when \(M_1\) is \(R\)-projective, and

\[\operatorname{Ext}^n_{RG}(M_1, M_3) \cong H^n(G, \operatorname{Hom}_R(M_1, M_3))\]

when \(M_1\) is \(R\)-projective.

When the trivial module is a direct summand of a tensor product. Decomposing \(M \otimes_k N\) into indecomposable summands is hard in general, but we can always tell when the trivial module \(k\) splits off as a direct summand. Suppose \(R = k\) is an algebraically closed field of characteristic \(p\) (possibly \(p = 0\)), and \(G\) is a group. If \(M\) and \(N\) are finite-dimensional indecomposable \(kG\)-modules, then \(M \otimes_k N\) has the trivial module \(k\) as a direct summand if and only if both of the following conditions hold: \(M \cong N^*\); and \(p mid \dim_k(N)\) (which holds automatically when \(p = 0\)).

Moreover, when \(k\) is a direct summand of \(N^* \otimes_k N\), it occurs with multiplicity one (so \(k \oplus k\) is never a direct summand). Intuitively, splitting off \(k\) inside \(N^* \otimes_k N \cong \operatorname{End}_k(N)\) requires a \(G\)-invariant map \(k o \operatorname{End}_k(N)\) and a \(G\)-invariant functional \(\operatorname{End}_k(N) o k\) whose composite is non-zero, and this composite is the matrix trace on the local ring \(\operatorname{End}_{kG}(N)\). Every endomorphism in \(\operatorname{End}_{kG}(N)\) has the form \(\lambda I + n\) with \(n\) nilpotent, whose trace \(\lambda \dim_k(N)\) can be non-zero if and only if \(p mid \dim_k(N)\).

Projectivity test via tensor products. If \(M\) is a finite-dimensional module for a cocommutative Hopf algebra \(\Lambda\) over a field \(k\), then \(M\) is a direct summand of \(M \otimes_k M^* \otimes_k M\), and the following five conditions are equivalent: \(M\) is projective; \(M \otimes_k M^*\) is projective; \(M \otimes_k M\) is projective; \(M^*\) is projective; and \(M\) is injective.

In particular, every finite-dimensional cocommutative Hopf algebra \(\Lambda\) over a field \(k\) is self-injective (this remains true even without cocommutativity, though the argument is harder). The reason \(M\) is a direct summand of \(M \otimes_k M^* \otimes_k M\) is that the coevaluation map \(k o M \otimes_k M^*\) (\(1 \mapsto \sum_i m_i \otimes m'_i\) in dual bases) and the evaluation map \(M^* \otimes_k M o k\) (\(m'_i \otimes m \mapsto m'_i(m)\)) compose to the identity on \(M\).

Worked example: decomposing \(V \otimes_{\mathbb{F}_p} V\) for the \(2\)-dimensional \(\mathbb{F}_p C_p\)-module in characteristic \(p = 2\) versus \(p = 3\). Let \(G = C_p = \langle a : a^p = 1 angle\) over \(k = \mathbb{F}_p\), and let \(V = M_2 = \mathbb{F}_p[x]/(x^2)\) (\(x = a - 1\)) be the \(2\)-dimensional indecomposable module from the uniserial modules \(M_j = \mathbb{F}_p[x]/(x^j)\) (where \(M_1 = \mathbb{F}_p\) is the trivial module and \(M_p = \mathbb{F}_p[x]/(x^p) \cong \mathbb{F}_p C_p\) is the free module of rank \(1\)), with basis \(e_1, e_2\) (\(ae_1 = e_1\), \(ae_2 = e_1 + e_2\)). We saw above that \(V \cong V^*\) and \(\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}(V) = 2\). When \(p = 2\), we have \(p \mid \dim_{\mathbb{F}_2}(V) = 2\), and \(V = \mathbb{F}_2 C_2\) is the free module of rank \(1\); here \((a - 1)\) has rank \(2\) and square \(0\) on \(V \otimes_{\mathbb{F}_2} V\), so \(V \otimes_{\mathbb{F}_2} V \cong M_2 \oplus M_2\) splits into two free summands of dimension \(2\) and has no trivial direct summand \(\mathbb{F}_2\).

When \(p = 3\), by contrast, \(p mid \dim_{\mathbb{F}_3}(V) = 2\): applying the theorem over an algebraic closure of \(\mathbb{F}_3\) (where \(V\) stays indecomposable because \(a - 1 eq 0\) has a single Jordan block) predicts a single trivial summand, and a direct computation confirms this over \(\mathbb{F}_3\) itself. Concretely, in \(V \otimes_{\mathbb{F}_3} V\), the vector \(w_1 = e_1 \otimes e_2 - e_2 \otimes e_1\) satisfies \(aw_1 = e_1 \otimes (e_1 + e_2) - (e_1 + e_2) \otimes e_1 = w_1\), spanning a \(1\)-dimensional trivial summand \(\mathbb{F}_3 w_1 \cong M_1\). Meanwhile, \(v = e_2 \otimes e_2\) satisfies \((a - 1)v = e_1 \otimes e_2 + e_2 \otimes e_1 + e_1 \otimes e_1\), \((a - 1)^2 v = 2(e_1 \otimes e_1) eq 0\) in \(\mathbb{F}_3\), and \((a - 1)^3 v = 0\), spanning a \(3\)-dimensional cyclic summand isomorphic to \(M_3 = \mathbb{F}_3 C_3\):

\[M_2 \otimes_{\mathbb{F}_3} M_2 \cong M_1 \oplus M_3 = \mathbb{F}_3 \oplus \mathbb{F}_3 C_3.\]

docs.title: Induction and Restriction
docs.text: In the previous chapter we studied restriction and induction for \(\mathbb{C}G\)-modules by embedding irreducible \(\mathbb{C}H\)-modules into the group algebra \(\mathbb{C}H\) and multiplying on the right by \(\mathbb{C}G\). Over an arbitrary commutative ring \(R\) (or a field of characteristic \(p\) dividing \(\lvert G\rvert\)), modules no longer split into irreducibles and need not embed inside \(RH\). How do we define induction and coinduction for any \(RH\)-module in one step using tensor products and \(\operatorname{Hom}\), why do the two coincide for finite groups, and how does an induced module decompose when restricted to a second subgroup?

docs.title: Tensor-Product Induction, Coinduction and Frobenius Reciprocity
docs.text:
Restriction and tensor-product induction. Let \(H\) be a subgroup of a finite group \(G\), so that \(RH\) is a subring of \(RG\). Any left \(RG\)-module \(M\) can be restricted to \(RH\) by keeping only the actions of elements of \(H\), written \(M{\downarrow_H}\) (restricting modules and characters to a subgroup). Conversely, given a left \(RH\)-module \(N\), we view \(RG\) as an \(RG\)-\(RH\)-bimodule (by left and right multiplication) and define the induced module \(N{\uparrow^G}\) to be the tensor product over \(RH\):

\[N{\uparrow^G} = RG \otimes_{RH} N.\]

Because \(RG\) is a free right \(RH\)-module of rank \(\lvert G : H\rvert\) on any set of left coset representatives \(g_i \in G/H\), the induced module decomposes as an \(R\)-module into \(\lvert G : H\rvert\) copies of \(N\):

\[N{\uparrow^G} = \bigoplus_{g_i \in G/H} g_i \otimes N.\]

To see how \(g \in G\) acts on the summand \(g_i \otimes N\), write \(gg_i = g_j h\) for the unique coset representative \(g_j \in G/H\) and \(h \in H\); sliding \(h\) across \(\otimes_{RH}\) gives \(g(g_i \otimes n) = (g_j h) \otimes n = g_j \otimes hn\). In particular, inducing the trivial \(RH\)-module \(R\) gives \(R{\uparrow^G} = RG \otimes_{RH} R \cong R(G/H)\), the permutation module on the left cosets \(G/H\).

Matching the submodule definition over \(\mathbb{C}\). In homomorphisms into the group algebra and inducing a module, induction was defined for a right \(\mathbb{C}H\)-submodule \(U \subseteq \mathbb{C}H\) as the subspace \(U(\mathbb{C}G) = \bigoplus_{i=1}^t U g_i \subseteq \mathbb{C}G\) spanned by right coset translates. For a left \(\mathbb{C}H\)-submodule \(N \subseteq \mathbb{C}H\), the multiplication map \(g_i \otimes n \mapsto g_i n\) identifies \(\mathbb{C}G \otimes_{\mathbb{C}H} N\) with the left ideal \((\mathbb{C}G)N = \bigoplus_{i=1}^t g_i N \subseteq \mathbb{C}G\), which is the exact left-module mirror image of \(U(\mathbb{C}G)\). Defining \(N{\uparrow^G} = RG \otimes_{RH} N\) as a tensor product has the advantage that it applies directly to every \(RH\)-module \(N\) over any ring \(R\) without decomposing \(N\) first.

Coinduction and duality. Using \(\operatorname{Hom}_{RH}\) instead of \(\otimes_{RH}\), the coinduced module of a left \(RH\)-module \(N\) is defined by

\[N{\Uparrow^G} = \operatorname{Hom}_{RH}(RG, N),\]

where \(RG\) is viewed as a left \(RH\)-module by left multiplication and \(g \in G\) acts on \(\phi \in \operatorname{Hom}_{RH}(RG, N)\) via \((g\phi)(x) = \phi(xg)\). For a finite group \(G\), the \(R\)-linear map \(\lambda : RG \to R\) sending \(\sum_{g \in G} r_g g \mapsto r_1\) induces an isomorphism \(RG \cong (RG)^* = \operatorname{Hom}_R(RG, R)\) of \(RG\)-\(RG\)-bimodules (sending \(g \in G\) to the functional that picks out the coefficient of \(g^{-1}\)). As a result, induction and restriction commute with taking duals,

\[(M^*){\downarrow_H} \cong (M{\downarrow_H})^* \qquad \text{and} \qquad (N^*){\uparrow^G} \cong (N{\uparrow^G})^*,\]

and induction and coinduction coincide:

\[N{\uparrow^G} = RG \otimes_{RH} N \cong (RG)^* \otimes_{RH} N \cong \operatorname{Hom}_{RH}(RG, N) = N{\Uparrow^G}.\]

Nakayama relations (Frobenius reciprocity for modules). For any \(RH\)-module \(N\) and any \(RG\)-module \(M\), there are natural isomorphisms of \(R\)-modules:

\[\operatorname{Hom}_{RH}(N, M{\downarrow_H}) \cong \operatorname{Hom}_{RG}(N{\uparrow^G}, M)\]

and

\[\operatorname{Hom}_{RH}(M{\downarrow_H}, N) \cong \operatorname{Hom}_{RG}(M, N{\uparrow^G})\]

These two adjunctions are the module-theoretic form of Frobenius reciprocity: induction \(-{\uparrow^G}\) is both the left adjoint (via tensor-Hom adjunction on \(RG \otimes_{RH} N\)) and the right adjoint (via \(N{\uparrow^G} \cong N{\Uparrow^G} = \operatorname{Hom}_{RH}(RG, N)\)) of restriction \(-{\downarrow_H}\). Explicitly, the second isomorphism \(\operatorname{Hom}_{RH}(M{\downarrow_H}, N) \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{Hom}_{RG}(M, N{\uparrow^G})\) is given by the exterior trace map \(\widehat{\operatorname{Tr}}_{H, G}\), defined for \(\phi \in \operatorname{Hom}_{RH}(M{\downarrow_H}, N)\) by

\[\widehat{\operatorname{Tr}}_{H, G}(\phi)(m) = \sum_{g \in G/H} g \otimes \phi(g^{-1}m),\]

where each summand \(g \otimes \phi(g^{-1}m)\) depends only on the left coset \(gH\) because \(h \in H\) slides across \(\otimes_{RH}\).

Projective modules and the Eckmann–Shapiro lemma. Because \(RG\) is a free \(RH\)-module of rank \(\lvert G : H\rvert\), restriction \(-{\downarrow_H}\) and induction \(-{\uparrow^G}\) are both exact functors, and both preserve projective modules (restricting a projective \(RG\)-module to \(H\) gives a projective \(RH\)-module, and inducing a projective \(RH\)-module to \(G\) gives a projective \(RG\)-module). Applying the Nakayama relations to projective resolutions therefore gives the Eckmann–Shapiro lemma for all \(n \ge 0\):

\[\operatorname{Ext}^n_{RH}(N, M{\downarrow_H}) \cong \operatorname{Ext}^n_{RG}(N{\uparrow^G}, M) \qquad \text{and} \qquad \operatorname{Ext}^n_{RH}(M{\downarrow_H}, N) \cong \operatorname{Ext}^n_{RG}(M, N{\uparrow^G}).\]

Induction of tensor products and \(\operatorname{Hom}\). Inducing a tensor product (or \(\operatorname{Hom}\)) in which one factor is restricted from \(G\) is the same as inducing the other factor first and then tensoring (or taking \(\operatorname{Hom}\)) over \(G\). Formally, if \(N\) is an \(RH\)-module and \(M\) is an \(RG\)-module, then there are natural isomorphisms of \(RG\)-modules:

\[(N \otimes_R M{\downarrow_H}){\uparrow^G} \cong N{\uparrow^G} \otimes_R M\]

and

\[\operatorname{Hom}_R(N, M{\downarrow_H}){\uparrow^G} \cong \operatorname{Hom}_R(N{\uparrow^G}, M)\]

In the first identity, the \(G\)-action on \(M\) extends across all of \(G\), so the shearing map \(g \otimes (n \otimes m) \mapsto (g \otimes n) \otimes gm\) (with inverse \((g \otimes n) \otimes m \mapsto g \otimes (n \otimes g^{-1}m)\)) untwists \(M{\downarrow_H}\) out of \(\otimes_{RH}\) into the diagonal tensor product \(N{\uparrow^G} \otimes_R M\), and the second identity is its counterpart under coinduction. Taking \(N = R\) gives \((M{\downarrow_H}){\uparrow^G} \cong R(G/H) \otimes_R M\).

docs.title: Conjugate Modules, Double Cosets and the Mackey Decomposition
docs.text:
Double cosets and conjugate modules. Now let \(H\) and \(K\) be two subgroups of \(G\), and suppose we induce an \(RK\)-module \(M\) to \(G\) and then restrict it to \(H\), forming \(M{\uparrow^G}{\downarrow_H} = {}_{RH}RG_{RK} \otimes_{RK} M\). Under left multiplication by \(H\) and right multiplication by \(K\), the group \(G\) breaks into disjoint double cosets \(HgK = \{hgk : h \in H,\, k \in K\}\), giving an \(RH\)-\(RK\)-bimodule decomposition

\[{}_{RH}RG_{RK} = \bigoplus_{HgK \in H \backslash G / K} R(HgK).\]

For each \(g \in G\), let \({}^g K = gKg^{-1}\) be the conjugate subgroup, and define the conjugate module \({}^g M\) (also written \(g \otimes M\)) to be the left \(R({}^g K)\)-module consisting of symbols \(g \otimes m\) (\(m \in M\)) with action

\[(gkg^{-1})(g \otimes m) = g \otimes km \qquad (k \in K,\; m \in M).\]

Each double coset bimodule \(R(HgK)\) is isomorphic to \(RH \otimes_{R(H \cap {}^g K)} (g \otimes RK)\) via \(hgk \leftrightarrow h \otimes (g \otimes k)\).

Mackey decomposition theorem. Inducing a module from \(K\) to \(G\) and restricting to \(H\) is the same as conjugating the module by each \((H, K)\)-double coset representative \(g\), restricting to the intersection \(H \cap {}^g K\), and inducing back up to \(H\). Formally, if \(H\) and \(K\) are subgroups of \(G\) and \(M\) is an \(RK\)-module, then as \(RH\)-modules,

\[M{\uparrow^G}{\downarrow_H} \cong \bigoplus_{HgK \in H \backslash G / K} ({}^g M){\downarrow_{H \cap {}^g K}}{\uparrow^H},\]

where the direct sum runs over a set of double coset representatives \(g\) for \(H \backslash G / K\). Intuitively, \(M{\uparrow^G}\) places a copy of \(M\) on each left coset in \(G/K\), and when \(H\) acts on \(G/K\) on the left, the cosets break into \(H\)-orbits indexed by the double cosets \(HgK\), where the stabilizer in \(H\) of the coset \(gK\) is \(H \cap gKg^{-1} = H \cap {}^g K\).

Consequences of the Mackey formula for two induced modules. If \(M\) is an \(RK\)-module and \(N\) is an \(RH\)-module, combining the Mackey decomposition with the tensor identity and the Eckmann–Shapiro lemma decomposes tensor products, \(\operatorname{Hom}\), \(\operatorname{Tor}\), and \(\operatorname{Ext}\) between \(M{\uparrow^G}\) and \(N{\uparrow^G}\) over the double cosets \(HgK \in H \backslash G / K\):

\[M{\uparrow^G} \otimes_R N{\uparrow^G} \cong \bigoplus_{HgK} \bigl(({}^g M){\downarrow_{H \cap {}^g K}} \otimes_R N{\downarrow_{H \cap {}^g K}}\bigr){\uparrow^G}\] \[\operatorname{Hom}_R(M{\uparrow^G}, N{\uparrow^G}) \cong \bigoplus_{HgK} \bigl(\operatorname{Hom}_R(({}^g M){\downarrow_{H \cap {}^g K}}, N{\downarrow_{H \cap {}^g K}})\bigr){\uparrow^G}\] \[M{\uparrow^G} \otimes_{RG} N{\uparrow^G} \cong \bigoplus_{HgK} \bigl(({}^g M){\downarrow_{H \cap {}^g K}} \otimes_{R(H \cap {}^g K)} N{\downarrow_{H \cap {}^g K}}\bigr)\] \[\operatorname{Hom}_{RG}(M{\uparrow^G}, N{\uparrow^G}) \cong \bigoplus_{HgK} \operatorname{Hom}_{R(H \cap {}^g K)}\bigl(({}^g M){\downarrow_{H \cap {}^g K}}, N{\downarrow_{H \cap {}^g K}}\bigr)\] \[\operatorname{Tor}_n^{RG}(M{\uparrow^G}, N{\uparrow^G}) \cong \bigoplus_{HgK} \operatorname{Tor}_n^{R(H \cap {}^g K)}\bigl(({}^g M){\downarrow_{H \cap {}^g K}}, N{\downarrow_{H \cap {}^g K}}\bigr)\]

and

\[\operatorname{Ext}^n_{RG}(M{\uparrow^G}, N{\uparrow^G}) \cong \bigoplus_{HgK} \operatorname{Ext}^n_{R(H \cap {}^g K)}\bigl(({}^g M){\downarrow_{H \cap {}^g K}}, N{\downarrow_{H \cap {}^g K}}\bigr)\]

Worked example: the Mackey formula for two subgroups of order \(2\) in \(S_3\). Let \(G = S_3\) (of order \(6\)), and let \(K = \{1, (1\,2)\}\) and \(H = \{1, (2\,3)\}\) be two distinct subgroups of order \(2\). First let us find the \((H, K)\)-double cosets \(HgK\) in \(S_3\). For \(g_1 = 1\), the double coset

\[H \cdot 1 \cdot K = \{1, (2\,3)\}\{1, (1\,2)\} = \{1, (1\,2), (2\,3), (1\,3\,2)\}\]

has \(4\) elements, and the intersection \(H \cap {}^{g_1} K = H \cap K = \{1\}\) is trivial. The remaining \(6 - 4 = 2\) elements of \(S_3\) form a second double coset with representative \(g_2 = (1\,3)\):

\[H(1\,3)K = \{(1\,3), (1\,2\,3)\}.\]

Conjugating \(K = \{1, (1\,2)\}\) by \(g_2 = (1\,3)\) gives \({}^{(1\,3)}K = (1\,3)\{1, (1\,2)\}(1\,3) = \{1, (2\,3)\} = H\), so the second intersection is \(H \cap {}^{(1\,3)}K = H \cap H = H\) (of order \(2\)). For any \(RK\)-module \(M\), the Mackey decomposition therefore has two summands:

\[M{\uparrow^{S_3}}{\downarrow_H} \cong ({}^1 M){\downarrow_{\{1\}}}{\uparrow^H} \;\oplus\; ({}^{(1\,3)} M){\downarrow_H}{\uparrow^H}.\]

To see this decomposition concretely, take the trivial \(RK\)-module \(M = R\). Then \(R{\uparrow^{S_3}} \cong R(S_3/K)\) is the permutation module of \(R\)-rank \(3\) with basis given by the three left cosets \(1K = \{1, (1\,2)\}\), \((2\,3)K = \{(2\,3), (1\,3\,2)\}\), and \((1\,3)K = \{(1\,3), (1\,2\,3)\}\). When restricted to \(H = \{1, (2\,3)\}\), the generator \((2\,3) \in H\) swaps the first two cosets \(1K \leftrightarrow (2\,3)K\) (whose union is the double coset \(H \cdot 1 \cdot K\)) and fixes the third coset \((1\,3)K\) (which is the double coset \(H(1\,3)K\)). Thus \(\operatorname{sp}_R(1K, (2\,3)K) \cong RH\) and \(\operatorname{sp}_R((1\,3)K) \cong R\), decomposing \(R(S_3/K){\downarrow_H} \cong RH \oplus R\), which matches the two Mackey summands \(R{\downarrow_{\{1\}}}{\uparrow^H} \cong RH\) and \(R{\downarrow_H}{\uparrow^H} \cong R\).

More generally, for any \(RK\)-module \(M\) that is free of rank \(d\) over \(R\), the left-hand side \(M{\uparrow^{S_3}}{\downarrow_H}\) has \(R\)-rank \(\lvert S_3 : K\rvert d = 3d\), while on the right-hand side the first summand has \(R\)-rank \(\lvert H : \{1\}\rvert d = 2d\) and the second summand has \(R\)-rank \(\lvert H : H\rvert d = d\), summing to \(2d + d = 3d\). Similarly, when \(H = K = \{1, (1\,2)\}\), the two \((K, K)\)-double cosets are \(K \cdot 1 \cdot K = \{1, (1\,2)\}\) of size \(2\) with \(K \cap {}^1 K = K\), and \(K(2\,3)K = \{(2\,3), (1\,3), (1\,2\,3), (1\,3\,2)\}\) of size \(4\) with \(K \cap {}^{(2\,3)}K = \{1\}\), giving \(M{\uparrow^{S_3}}{\downarrow_K} \cong M \oplus ({}^{(2\,3)}M){\downarrow_{\{1\}}}{\uparrow^K}\) of \(R\)-rank \(d + 2d = 3d\). Figure 22 shows the three left cosets of \(K\) in \(S_3\) and how the action of \(H = \{1, (2\,3)\}\) groups them into the two double-coset orbits.

Figure 22. Mackey decomposition of \(M{\uparrow^{S_3}}{\downarrow_H}\) for \(G = S_3\), \(K = \{1, (1\,2)\}\), and \(H = \{1, (2\,3)\}\). (a) The induced module \(M{\uparrow^{S_3}} = RS_3 \otimes_{RK} M\) consists of three copies \(1 \otimes M\), \((2\,3) \otimes M\), and \((1\,3) \otimes M\) of \(M\), one over each left coset \(1K = \{1, (1\,2)\}\), \((2\,3)K = \{(2\,3), (1\,3\,2)\}\), and \((1\,3)K = \{(1\,3), (1\,2\,3)\}\). (b) Restricting to \(H = \{1, (2\,3)\}\) partitions the three coset boxes into two \(H\)-orbits corresponding to the \((H, K)\)-double cosets: \((2\,3)\) swaps \(1K\) and \((2\,3)K\) inside \(H \cdot 1 \cdot K = \{1, (1\,2), (2\,3), (1\,3\,2)\}\) (orbit of size \(2\) with trivial stabiliser \(H \cap {}^1 K = \{1\}\), giving \(({}^1 M){\downarrow_{\{1\}}}{\uparrow^H}\), or \(RH\) for \(M = R\)) and fixes \((1\,3)K\) inside \(H(1\,3)K = \{(1\,3), (1\,2\,3)\}\) (orbit of size \(1\) with full stabiliser \(H \cap {}^{(1\,3)}K = H\), giving \(({}^{(1\,3)}M){\downarrow_H}\), or \(R\) for \(M = R\)).

docs.title: Standard Resolutions
docs.text: Group cohomology \(H^n(G, M) = \operatorname{Ext}^n_{RG}(R, M)\) and group homology \(H_n(G, M) = \operatorname{Tor}_n^{RG}(M, R)\) were defined in group rings, representations, lattices and fixed points (built from defining Tor, Ext and general derived functors and augmented algebras) using any projective resolution of the trivial \(RG\)-module \(R\). To write down explicit cocycles and coboundaries that work for every group \(G\) at once, we need a canonical free resolution of \(R\) built directly from the elements of \(G\). How is this standard (or bar) resolution constructed, how does it turn \(n\)-cochains into functions \(G^n \to M\), and when can we replace it by a small periodic resolution?

docs.title: The Homogeneous and Bar Resolutions and Cochains on \(G^n\)
docs.text:
Standard resolution in homogeneous form. Let \(G\) be a group and \(R\) be a commutative ring. The standard resolution of \(R\) as a left \(RG\)-module is the sequence \(\cdots \to F_2 \xrightarrow{\partial_2} F_1 \xrightarrow{\partial_1} F_0 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} R \to 0\) in which \(F_n\) (\(n \ge 0\)) is the free \(R\)-module on all \((n + 1)\)-tuples \((g_0, g_1, \dots, g_n)\) of elements of \(G\), with diagonal left \(G\)-action \(g(g_0, \dots, g_n) = (gg_0, \dots, gg_n)\), augmentation \(\varepsilon(g_0) = 1\), and simplicial boundary map

\[\partial_n(g_0, \dots, g_n) = \sum_{i=0}^n (-1)^i (g_0, \dots, \widehat{g_i}, \dots, g_n),\]

where \(\widehat{g_i}\) indicates that \(g_i\) is omitted from the list. Each \(\partial_n\) is an \(RG\)-module homomorphism satisfying \(\partial_{n-1} \circ \partial_n = 0\). The augmented complex is exact because the \(R\)-linear map \(h_n : F_n \to F_{n+1}\) defined by \(h_n(g_0, \dots, g_n) = (1, g_0, \dots, g_n)\) (with \(h_{-1}(1) = (1)\)) satisfies \(\partial_{n+1} \circ h_n + h_{n-1} \circ \partial_n = \mathrm{id}_{F_n}\) and is therefore a chain contraction of the complex over \(R\).

Bar notation and the bar resolution. Because \(G\) acts freely on the leading coordinate \(g_0\) of \((g_0, \dots, g_n)\), we can factor \(g_0\) out on the left and record the \(n\) consecutive steps \(g_0^{-1}g_1, g_1^{-1}g_2, \dots, g_{n-1}^{-1}g_n\). In the bar notation, we set

\[[g_1 \mid g_2 \mid \dots \mid g_n] = (1,\, g_1,\, g_1 g_2,\, \dots,\, g_1 g_2 \cdots g_n) \in F_n, \qquad (g_0, \dots, g_n) = g_0[g_0^{-1}g_1 \mid g_1^{-1}g_2 \mid \dots \mid g_{n-1}^{-1}g_n].\]

Thus \(F_n\) is a free left \(RG\)-module of rank \(\lvert G\rvert^n\) with \(RG\)-basis consisting of the symbols \([g_1 \mid \dots \mid g_n]\) (\(g_i \in G\)), and \(F_0 \cong RG\) is free of rank \(1\) on the empty symbol \([\ ] = (1)\). For this reason, the standard resolution is also called the bar resolution. Rewriting \(\partial_n\) on the basis elements \([g_1 \mid \dots \mid g_n]\) gives the bar boundary formula:

\[\partial_n[g_1 \mid \dots \mid g_n] = g_1[g_2 \mid \dots \mid g_n] + \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} (-1)^i [g_1 \mid \dots \mid g_i g_{i+1} \mid \dots \mid g_n] + (-1)^n [g_1 \mid \dots \mid g_{n-1}].\]

In degrees \(1\), \(2\), and \(3\), the bar boundary maps are:

\[\partial_1[g_1] = g_1[\ ] - [\ ] = (g_1 - 1)[\ ]\] \[\partial_2[g_1 \mid g_2] = g_1[g_2] - [g_1 g_2] + [g_1]\]

and

\[\partial_3[g_1 \mid g_2 \mid g_3] = g_1[g_2 \mid g_3] - [g_1 g_2 \mid g_3] + [g_1 \mid g_2 g_3] - [g_1 \mid g_2]\]

Cochains on \(G^n\) and low-degree coboundaries. Applying \(M \otimes_{RG} -\) and \(\operatorname{Hom}_{RG}(-, M)\) to the bar resolution \(\mathbf{F}\) computes group homology and cohomology as

\[H_n(G, M) = \operatorname{Tor}_n^{RG}(M, R) = H_n(M \otimes_{RG} \mathbf{F},\, 1 \otimes \partial_*) \qquad \text{and} \qquad H^n(G, M) = \operatorname{Ext}^n_{RG}(R, M) = H^n(\operatorname{Hom}_{RG}(\mathbf{F}, M),\, \delta^*),\]

where \((\delta^n \alpha)(x) = \alpha(\partial_{n+1}x)\). Because \(F_n\) is the free \(RG\)-module on the bar symbols \([g_1 \mid \dots \mid g_n] \in G^n\), we have \(\operatorname{Hom}_{RG}(F_n, M) \cong \operatorname{Hom}_R(R[G^n], M)\), so a bar \(n\)-cochain \(\alpha \in \operatorname{Hom}_{RG}(F_n, M)\) is simply a function \(\alpha : G^n \to M\) (with \(\alpha([\ ]) \in M\) in degree \(0\)), and its coboundary \(\delta^n \alpha : G^{n+1} \to M\) is

\[(\delta^n \alpha)(g_1, \dots, g_{n+1}) = g_1 \alpha(g_2, \dots, g_{n+1}) + \sum_{i=1}^n (-1)^i \alpha(g_1, \dots, g_i g_{i+1}, \dots, g_{n+1}) + (-1)^{n+1} \alpha(g_1, \dots, g_n).\]

In degrees \(0\), \(1\), and \(2\), this formula gives the low-degree coboundary maps:

\[(\delta^0 m)(g_1) = g_1 m - m\]

for \(m = \alpha([\ ]) \in M\),

\[(\delta^1 \beta)(g_1, g_2) = g_1 \beta(g_2) - \beta(g_1 g_2) + \beta(g_1)\]

for \(\beta : G \to M\), and

\[(\delta^2 \alpha)(g_1, g_2, g_3) = g_1 \alpha(g_2, g_3) - \alpha(g_1 g_2, g_3) + \alpha(g_1, g_2 g_3) - \alpha(g_1, g_2)\]

for \(\alpha : G \times G \to M\).

docs.title: Diagonal Approximation, Inflation and Periodic Resolutions for Cyclic Groups
docs.text:
Cup products, diagonal approximations and the Alexander–Whitney map. Suppose \(\Lambda\) is a Hopf algebra over \(R\) that is projective as an \(R\)-module. Given \(\Lambda\)-modules \(M, M', N, N'\) that are projective over \(R\), tensoring an \(m\)-fold extension of \(M\) by \(M'\) with an \(n\)-fold extension of \(N\) by \(N'\) over \(R\) defines an associative cup product \(\cup : \operatorname{Ext}^m_\Lambda(M, M') imes \operatorname{Ext}^n_\Lambda(N, N') o \operatorname{Ext}^{m+n}_\Lambda(M \otimes_R N, M' \otimes_R N')\). When \(\Lambda\) is cocommutative, the cup product is graded commutative (\(\alpha \cup eta = (-1)^{mn} eta \cup \alpha\) up to the twist \(M' \otimes_R N' \cong N' \otimes_R M'\)), making \(H^*(\Lambda, R) = \operatorname{Ext}^*_\Lambda(R, R)\) a graded-commutative ring; on \(\operatorname{Ext}^*_\Lambda(R, R)\), the cup product agrees with Yoneda composition.

To compute cup products on \(H^*(\Lambda, -)\) from a projective resolution \(\mathbf{P} o R\), one uses a diagonal approximation, meaning a chain map \(\Delta : \mathbf{P} o \mathbf{P} \otimes_R \mathbf{P}\) of \(\Lambda\)-modules lifting the isomorphism \(R \cong R \otimes_R R\) (which exists and is unique up to chain homotopy by the comparison theorem, and is homotopy co-associative and homotopy cocommutative). On the standard resolution \(\mathbf{F}\) of \(R\) over \(RG\), a strictly co-associative diagonal approximation is given by the Alexander–Whitney map \(\Delta : \mathbf{F} o \mathbf{F} \otimes_R \mathbf{F}\):

\[\Delta(g_0, \dots, g_n) = \sum_{j=0}^n (g_0, \dots, g_j) \otimes (g_j, \dots, g_n), \qquad \Delta[g_1 \mid \dots \mid g_n] = \sum_{j=0}^n [g_1 \mid \dots \mid g_j] \otimes g_1 \cdots g_j[g_{j+1} \mid \dots \mid g_n].\]

Pulling cochains \(\alpha : G^m o M\) and \( eta : G^n o N\) back along \(\Delta\) gives the explicit cochain formula for the cup product \(\alpha \cup eta : G^{m+n} o M \otimes_R N\):

\[(\alpha \cup eta)(g_1, \dots, g_{m+n}) = \alpha(g_1, \dots, g_m) \otimes g_1 \cdots g_m\, eta(g_{m+1}, \dots, g_{m+n}).\]

Restriction, inflation and the five-term exact sequence. For any subgroup \(H \le G\), restricting a projective resolution of an \(RG\)-module \(M\) to \(RH\) gives a projective resolution of \(M{\downarrow_H}\) over \(RH\), which induces the restriction map \(\operatorname{res}_{G, H} : \operatorname{Ext}^n_{RG}(M, M') o \operatorname{Ext}^n_{RH}(M{\downarrow_H}, M'{\downarrow_H})\) and in particular \(\operatorname{res}_{G, H} : H^n(G, M) o H^n(H, M{\downarrow_H})\); on bar cochains, \(\operatorname{res}_{G, H}\) simply restricts a function \(G^n o M\) to \(H^n o M\).

Now suppose \(N\) is a normal subgroup of \(G\) and \(M\) is an \(RG\)-module. When \(N\) acts trivially on \(M\), \(M\) is an \(R(G/N)\)-module: if \(\mathbf{P}\) is a projective resolution of \(R\) over \(R(G/N)\) and \(\mathbf{Q}\) is a projective resolution of \(R\) over \(RG\), viewing \(\mathbf{P}\) as a complex of \(RG\)-modules via \(G woheadrightarrow G/N\) and applying the comparison theorem lifts \(\mathrm{id}_R\) to a chain map \( ho : \mathbf{Q} o \mathbf{P}\) unique up to homotopy, and composing cocycles \(\hat{\zeta} : P_n o M\) with \( ho\) defines the inflation map \(\operatorname{inf}_{G/N, G} : H^n(G/N, M) o H^n(G, M)\) (on bar cochains, inflated cochains are functions on \(G^n\) that are constant on \(N\)-cosets). More generally, for any \(RG\)-module \(M\), the fixed-point submodule \(M^N\) has trivial \(N\)-action, and we write \(\operatorname{inf}_{G/N, G} : H^n(G/N, M^N) o H^n(G, M)\) for the composite \(H^n(G/N, M^N) o H^n(G, M^N) o H^n(G, M)\) with the map induced by \(M^N \hookrightarrow M\).

Computing \(H^*(N, M)\) using the \(RG\)-resolution \(\mathbf{Q}\) of \(R\) gives an action of the quotient group \(G/N\) on \(H^*(N, M)\) such that the image of \(\operatorname{res}_{G, N} : H^*(G, M) o H^*(N, M)\) lies in the fixed points \(H^*(N, M)^{G/N}\); explicitly, in degree \(1\), an element \(g \in G\) acts on a \(1\)-cocycle \( eta : N o M\) by \((g eta)(n) = g eta(g^{-1}ng)\), and for \(g \in N\) this changes \( eta\) only by the \(1\)-coboundary \(n \mapsto n\, eta(g) - eta(g)\). For any \(RG\)-module \(M\), combining inflation and restriction with the transgression map \(H^1(N, M)^{G/N} o H^2(G/N, M^N)\) gives the five-term exact sequence in low degrees:

\[0 o H^1(G/N, M^N) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{inf}} H^1(G, M) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{res}} H^1(N, M)^{G/N} o H^2(G/N, M^N) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{inf}} H^2(G, M).\]

This exact sequence does not continue to higher degrees.

Periodic resolution and cohomology of a cyclic group. Because \(\operatorname{rank}_{RG}(F_n) = \lvert G vert^n\) grows exponentially with \(n\), the bar resolution is replaced whenever possible by a smaller resolution. For a cyclic group \(C_m = \langle x : x^m = 1 angle\) of order \(m\) over any commutative ring \(R\) (generalising our periodic resolution over \(kC_p\)), define two \(RC_m\)-module endomorphisms of the free module \(RC_m\) of rank \(1\), the norm map \( u\) and the difference map \(T\):

\[ u : RC_m o RC_m, \quad u \mapsto (1 + x + \cdots + x^{m-1})u, \qquad T : RC_m o RC_m, \quad u \mapsto (1 - x)u.\]

The \(2\)-periodic sequence

\[\cdots \xrightarrow{ u} RC_m \xrightarrow{T} RC_m \xrightarrow{ u} RC_m \xrightarrow{T} RC_m \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} R o 0\]

is a free resolution of \(R\) as an \(RC_m\)-module, because in the \(R\)-basis \(1, x, \dots, x^{m-1}\) the elements killed by \(1 - x\) are the constant sums (\(\operatorname{Im}( u)\)) and the elements killed by \(1 + x + \cdots + x^{m-1}\) are the sums whose coefficients add to \(0\) (\(\operatorname{Im}(T)\)).

Applying \(\operatorname{Hom}_{RC_m}(-, M)\) to this resolution identifies \(\operatorname{Hom}_{RC_m}(RC_m, M) \cong M\) in every degree and turns the differentials into alternating multiplications by \(1 - x\) and \(1 + x + \cdots + x^{m-1}\) on \(M\), giving the cohomology of \(C_m\) for all degrees:

\[H^0(C_m, M) = M^{C_m} = \{v \in M : (1 - x)v = 0\},\] \[H^{2r}(C_m, M) = M^{C_m} / (1 + x + \cdots + x^{m-1})M \qquad (r > 0),\] \[H^{2r+1}(C_m, M) = \{v \in M : (1 + x + \cdots + x^{m-1})v = 0\} / (1 - x)M \qquad (r \ge 0).\]

Worked example: cohomology of \(C_2\) on \(\mathbb{Z}\) with trivial and sign actions. Take \(G = C_2 = \langle x : x^2 = 1 angle\) over \(R = \mathbb{Z}\). On the trivial module \(M = \mathbb{Z}\) (\(x \cdot m = m\)), the map \(1 - x\) is \(0\) and \(1 + x\) is multiplication by \(2\), so \(H^0(C_2, \mathbb{Z}) = \mathbb{Z}\), \(H^{2r}(C_2, \mathbb{Z}) = \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\) for \(r > 0\), and \(H^{2r+1}(C_2, \mathbb{Z}) = 0\) for \(r \ge 0\). On the sign module \(M = \mathbb{Z}_-\) where \(x\) acts on \(\mathbb{Z}\) by \(-1\), the map \(1 - x\) is multiplication by \(2\) and \(1 + x\) is \(0\), so \(H^0(C_2, \mathbb{Z}_-) = 0\), \(H^{2r}(C_2, \mathbb{Z}_-) = 0\) for \(r > 0\), and \(H^{2r+1}(C_2, \mathbb{Z}_-) = \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\) for \(r \ge 0\).

More generally, if \(H rianglelefteq G\) is a normal subgroup with cyclic quotient \(G/H\) and \(M\) is an \(RG\)-module whose restriction \(M{\downarrow_H}\) is projective, tensoring \(M\) with the two-step exact sequence \(0 o R o R(G/H) \xrightarrow{T} R(G/H) o R o 0\) keeps the middle terms projective over \(RG\) and gives \(M \oplus ( ext{projective}) \cong ilde{\Omega}^2(M) \oplus ( ext{projective})\).

docs.title: Low Degree Cohomology
docs.text: Building a group \(\hat{G}\) from an abelian normal subgroup \(M\) and a quotient group \(G \cong \hat{G}/M\) requires an action of \(G\) on \(M\) and a factor set measuring how coset representatives slip when multiplied (both are made precise below). A note on wording: the example of building a larger group calls a group with normal subgroup \(N\) and quotient \(Q\) an extension of \(N\) by \(Q\), whereas here we follow the opposite convention and call \(1 \to M \to \hat{G} \to G \to 1\) an extension of the quotient \(G\) by the normal subgroup \(M\). Now that we have defined \(H^n(G, M) \cong \operatorname{Ext}^n_{RG}(R, M) \cong \operatorname{Ext}^n_{\mathbb{Z}G}(\mathbb{Z}, M)\) and written out the low-degree differentials on the bar resolution, we can make that picture precise. What do \(H^0(G, M)\), \(H^1(G, M)\), and \(H^2(G, M)\) classify in group theory, and how does \(H^2\) govern lifting modular representations to characteristic zero?

docs.title: Degree Zero, Derivations, Split Extensions and Complements
docs.text:
Degree zero cohomology and derivations in degree one. On the bar resolution, a \(0\)-cochain is an element \(m \in M\) with coboundary \((\delta^0 m)(g) = gm - m\), so \(H^0(G, M) = \operatorname{Ker}(\delta^0) = M^G\) is the submodule of \(G\)-fixed points. In degree \(1\), a \(1\)-cochain \(\beta : G \to M\) satisfies \((\delta^1 \beta)(g_1, g_2) = g_1 \beta(g_2) - \beta(g_1 g_2) + \beta(g_1) = 0\) if and only if

\[\beta(g_1 g_2) = \beta(g_1) + g_1 \beta(g_2) \qquad (g_1, g_2 \in G).\]

A function \(\beta : G \to M\) obeying this twisted product rule is called a derivation (or crossed homomorphism) from \(G\) to \(M\), while a \(1\)-coboundary \((\delta^0 m)(g) = gm - m\) (\(m \in M\)) is called an inner derivation (or principal derivation). Thus \(H^1(G, M)\) is the quotient group of derivations modulo inner derivations.

Worked examples: \(H^1(G, M) = \operatorname{Hom}(G, M)\) for trivial action, and \(H^1(C_2, \mathbb{Z}_-) \cong \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\) from derivations. First, suppose \(G\) acts trivially on \(M\), so \(gm = m\) for all \(g \in G\) and \(m \in M\). Then the derivation rule reduces to \(\beta(g_1 g_2) = \beta(g_1) + \beta(g_2)\), which is an ordinary group homomorphism from \(G\) to the additive group of \(M\), while every inner derivation \(g \mapsto gm - m = 0\) vanishes identically. Thus when \(G\) acts trivially on \(M\),

\[H^1(G, M) = \operatorname{Hom}(G, M),\]

and because \(M\) is abelian, every homomorphism \(G \to M\) contains the commutator subgroup \([G, G]\) in its kernel (taking \(M = R\) gives \(\operatorname{Ext}^1_{RG}(R, R) \cong \operatorname{Hom}(G, R^+)\)).

Second, let \(G = C_2 = \{1, x\}\) (\(x^2 = 1\)) act on \(M = \mathbb{Z}_-\) by \(x \cdot m = -m\). For any derivation \(\beta : C_2 \to \mathbb{Z}_-\), evaluating at \(1 = 1 \cdot 1\) gives \(\beta(1) = \beta(1) + \beta(1)\), so \(\beta(1) = 0\), and evaluating at \(1 = x^2\) gives

\[0 = \beta(1) = \beta(x^2) = \beta(x) + x \cdot \beta(x) = \beta(x) - \beta(x) = 0,\]

which holds for every integer \(\beta(x) \in \mathbb{Z}\). Thus the group of derivations \(C_2 \to \mathbb{Z}_-\) is isomorphic to \(\mathbb{Z}\) via \(\beta \mapsto \beta(x)\). Meanwhile, the inner derivation \(\delta^0(m)\) for \(m \in \mathbb{Z}_-\) sends \(1 \mapsto 0\) and \(x \mapsto x \cdot m - m = -2m\), so the inner derivations are those with \(\beta(x) \in 2\mathbb{Z}\), giving \(H^1(C_2, \mathbb{Z}_-) \cong \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\), in agreement with the periodic resolution.

Group extensions, central extensions and split extensions. A group extension of a group \(G\) by an \(RG\)-module \(M\) is a short exact sequence of groups

\[1 \to M \to \hat{G} \to G \to 1\]

in which \(M\) is regarded as an abelian normal subgroup of \(\hat{G}\) (written multiplicatively inside \(\hat{G}\)) and the conjugation action of \(G\) on \(M\) inside \(\hat{G}\) coincides with the module action of \(G\) on \(M\). A central extension of \(G\) is a group extension in which \(G\) acts trivially on \(M\) (so \(M \le Z(\hat{G})\)), and an isomorphism of group extensions is a group isomorphism \(\hat{G}_1 \xrightarrow{\sim} \hat{G}_2\) that induces the identity map on both \(M\) and \(G\). The extension is a split group extension (or splits) if \(\hat{G}\) contains a subgroup complementary to \(M\), so that \(\hat{G} \cong M \rtimes G\) is a semidirect product whose elements may be written as lower-triangular matrices \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ m & g \end{pmatrix}\) (\(m \in M, g \in G\)) multiplying by

\[\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ m_1 & g_1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ m_2 & g_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ m_1 + g_1 m_2 & g_1 g_2 \end{pmatrix}.\]

Classification of complements by \(H^1(G, M)\). The cohomology group \(H^1(G, M)\) parametrises the set of conjugacy classes of complements to the normal subgroup \(M\) in the split extension \(\hat{G} = M \rtimes G\). Specifically, a complement to \(M\) in \(\hat{G}\) is a subgroup consisting of one matrix \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ \beta[g] & g \end{pmatrix}\) for each \(g \in G\), where \(\beta : G \to M\) is a derivation (\(1\)-cocycle), and conjugating the complement by an element of \(\hat{G}\) shifts \(\beta\) by an inner derivation (\(1\)-coboundary).

In module-extension terms, \(\hat{G}\) acts on \(\hat{M} = R \oplus M\) via \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ m_1 & g \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} n \\ m_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} n \\ nm_1 + gm_2 \end{pmatrix}\), forming a short exact sequence \(0 \to M \to \hat{M} \to R \to 0\). Two complements to \(M\) in \(\hat{G}\) are conjugate if and only if restricting \(0 \to M \to \hat{M} \to R \to 0\) to each complement gives the same extension class in \(\operatorname{Ext}^1_{RG}(R, M)\).

docs.title: Degree Two Cohomology, Factor Sets and Group Extensions
docs.text:
Classification of group extensions by \(H^2(G, M)\) and factor sets. The cohomology group \(H^2(G, M)\) parametrises the set of isomorphism classes of extensions \(1 \to M \to \hat{G} \to G \to 1\) of \(G\) by the \(RG\)-module \(M\). Choosing a coset representative \(\hat{g} \in \hat{G}\) for each \(g \in G\) defines a function \(\alpha : G \times G \to M\) by \(\hat{g}_1 \hat{g}_2 = \alpha[g_1 \mid g_2]\widehat{g_1 g_2}\), which is called the factor set and gives the group multiplication on pairs \((m, g) \in M \times G\):

\[(m_1, g_1)(m_2, g_2) = \bigl(m_1 + g_1(m_2) + \alpha[g_1 \mid g_2],\, g_1 g_2\bigr).\]

Associativity in \(\hat{G}\) is the \(2\)-cocycle equation \(\alpha[g_1 \mid g_2] + \alpha[g_1 g_2 \mid g_3] = g_1\alpha[g_2 \mid g_3] + \alpha[g_1 \mid g_2 g_3]\) (\(\delta^2 \alpha = 0\)), and changing coset representatives to \(\tilde{g} = \beta[g]\hat{g}\) shifts \(\alpha[g_1 \mid g_2]\) by the \(2\)-coboundary \(\beta[g_1] + g_1\beta[g_2] - \beta[g_1 g_2]\).

Aside: how a \(2\)-fold module extension builds a group extension of \(3 \times 3\) block matrices.

Suppose a \(2\)-fold module extension \(0 \to M \to A \to B \to R \to 0\) represents a class in \(\operatorname{Ext}^2_{RG}(R, M) \cong H^2(G, M)\), and let \(M' = \operatorname{Coker}(M \to A) \cong \operatorname{Ker}(B \to R)\) be its image-kernel module in the middle. This \(2\)-fold extension is the Yoneda splice of two short exact sequences \(0 \to M \to A \to M' \to 0\) and \(0 \to M' \to B \to R \to 0\). When these two short exact sequences split as \(R\)-modules (\(A \cong M' \oplus M\) and \(B \cong R \oplus M'\) over \(R\)), the action of \(g \in G\) on \(A\) and on \(B\) takes lower-triangular block-matrix form:

\[A(g) = \begin{pmatrix} \phi_{M'}(g) & 0 \\ a(g) & \phi_M(g) \end{pmatrix}, \qquad B(g) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ b(g) & \phi_{M'}(g) \end{pmatrix},\]

where \(\phi_M(g)\) and \(\phi_{M'}(g)\) are the actions of \(g\) on \(M\) and \(M'\), while \(a(g) \in \operatorname{Hom}_R(M', M)\) and \(b(g) \in \operatorname{Hom}_R(R, M') \cong M'\) measure how \(g\) mixes the quotient into the submodule in each step.

Now fit \(B(g)\) in the top-left \(2 \times 2\) corner and \(A(g)\) in the bottom-right \(2 \times 2\) corner of a \(3 \times 3\) block matrix by leaving the bottom-left corner \(* \in \operatorname{Hom}_R(R, M) \cong M\) completely free:

\[\hat{G} = \left\{ \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ b(g) & \phi_{M'}(g) & 0 \\ * & a(g) & \phi_M(g) \end{pmatrix} : g \in G,\; * \in M \right\}.\]

Because \(A\) and \(B\) are \(RG\)-modules, multiplying two such \(3 \times 3\) matrices for \(g_1\) and \(g_2\) reproduces \(b(g_1 g_2)\) and \(a(g_1 g_2)\) along the subdiagonal and adds an extra term \(a(g_1)b(g_2) \in M\) into the bottom-left corner \(*\). The matrices with \(g = 1\) (so \(\phi_{M'}(1) = \mathrm{id}_{M'}\), \(\phi_M(1) = \mathrm{id}_M\), \(a(1) = 0\), \(b(1) = 0\)) and \(* \in M\) form an abelian normal subgroup isomorphic to \(M\), and projecting onto \(g \in G\) makes \(\hat{G}\) a group extension \(1 \to M \to \hat{G} \to G \to 1\).

Splitting this group extension means choosing a specific bottom-left entry \(* = c(g) \in M\) for each \(g \in G\) so that the resulting \(3 \times 3\) matrices close under multiplication, which is equivalent to the Yoneda splice of \(0 \to M \to A \to M' \to 0\) and \(0 \to M' \to B \to R \to 0\) representing the zero class in \(\operatorname{Ext}^2_{RG}(R, M)\). Moreover, a second choice \(c(g) + c'(g)\) also gives a splitting if and only if the \(2 \times 2\) block matrix \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ c'(g) & \phi_M(g) \end{pmatrix}\) defines a module extension in \(\operatorname{Ext}^1_{RG}(R, M) = H^1(G, M)\), so the splittings in the matrix picture differ by \(1\)-cocycles.

Worked example: \(H^2(C_2, \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}) \cong \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\) and the extensions \(C_2 \times C_2\) versus \(C_4\). Let \(G = C_2 = \{1, x\}\) (\(x^2 = 1\)) act trivially on \(M = \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} = \{0, 1\}\). By our cyclic-group cohomology formula (where \(1 - x = 0\) and \(1 + x = 2 \equiv 0 \pmod{2}\) on \(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\)),

\[H^2(C_2, \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}) = (\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^{C_2} / 2(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}) = \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}.\]

On the bar resolution, choosing the identity representative \(\hat{1} = 1 \in \hat{G}\) normalises \(\alpha[1 \mid 1] = \alpha[1 \mid x] = \alpha[x \mid 1] = 0\), and changing the representative \(\hat{x}\) to \(\tilde{x} = \beta(x)\hat{x}\) cannot alter \(\alpha[x \mid x]\) because \((\delta^1\beta)(x, x) = 2\beta(x) - \beta(1) = 0 \pmod{2}\). Thus the cohomology class is determined by the single value \(\alpha[x \mid x] \in \{0, 1\}\), which records whether the square of \(\hat{x} = (0, x)\) in \(\hat{G}\) equals the identity \((0, 1)\) or slips into the non-zero kernel element \((1, 1)\). Setting \(\alpha[x \mid x] = 0\) gives \((0, x)^2 = (0, 1)\) and the split extension \(\hat{G} \cong (\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}) \times C_2 = V_4\) (the Klein four-group), whereas setting \(\alpha[x \mid x] = 1\) gives \((0, x)^2 = (1, 1) \neq (0, 1)\) of order \(4\) and the non-split cyclic extension \(\hat{G} \cong C_4\). Figure 23 illustrates the homogeneous bar simplices behind the \(2\)-cocycle condition and the two resulting extensions \(V_4\) and \(C_4\).

Figure 23. Simplicial picture of the bar \(2\)-cocycle condition and the two extensions of \(C_2 = \{1, x\}\) by \(M = \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} = \{0, 1\}\). (a) In the homogeneous standard resolution, a bar \(2\)-cochain \(\alpha\) assigns \(\alpha(g_1, g_2)\) to the triangle \([g_1 \mid g_2] = (1, g_1, g_1 g_2)\) with boundary \(\partial_2[g_1 \mid g_2] = g_1[g_2] - [g_1 g_2] + [g_1]\) (left), and the four triangular faces of the tetrahedron \([g_1 \mid g_2 \mid g_3] = (1, g_1, g_1 g_2, g_1 g_2 g_3)\) carry the four signed terms of the \(2\)-cocycle condition \((\delta^2\alpha)(g_1, g_2, g_3) = g_1\alpha(g_2, g_3) - \alpha(g_1 g_2, g_3) + \alpha(g_1, g_2 g_3) - \alpha(g_1, g_2) = 0\), where the face \((g_1, g_1 g_2, g_1 g_2 g_3)\) opposite vertex \(1\) is \(g_1\) times the triangle \((1, g_2, g_2 g_3)\) and so carries the factor \(g_1\) (right). (b) The four elements \((m, g)\) of \(\hat{G}\) drawn as two fibres of two points over \(1\) and \(x\) in \(C_2\): starting at \((0, 1) = \hat{1}\) and multiplying twice by the coset representative \(\hat{x} = (0, x)\) returns to \((0, 1)\) after two steps when \(\alpha[x \mid x] = 0\) (\(\hat{G} \cong V_4 = C_2 \times C_2\), left), whereas when \(\alpha[x \mid x] = 1\) the second step slips along the fibre over \(1\) to \(\hat{x}^2 = (1, 1)\) and two further steps via \((1, x)\) return to \((0, 1)\) (\(\hat{G} \cong C_4\), right).

docs.title: Splitting When \(\lvert G\rvert\) Is Invertible, Central Extensions and Lifting Theorems
docs.text:
Transfer and splitting of extensions when \(\lvert G\rvert\) is invertible. For any \(RG\)-modules \(M\) and \(M'\) and any subgroup \(H \le G\), composing the exterior trace map \(\widehat{\operatorname{Tr}}_{H, G} : \operatorname{Hom}_{RH}(M{\downarrow_H}, M'{\downarrow_H}) \to \operatorname{Hom}_{RG}(M, M'{\downarrow_H}{\uparrow^G})\) with the natural surjection \(M'{\downarrow_H}{\uparrow^G} \twoheadrightarrow M'\) (\(g \otimes m' \mapsto gm'\)) and applying the composite degreewise to a projective resolution defines the transfer map \(\operatorname{Tr}_{H, G} : \operatorname{Ext}^n_{RH}(M{\downarrow_H}, M'{\downarrow_H}) \to \operatorname{Ext}^n_{RG}(M, M')\), which satisfies \(\operatorname{Tr}_{H, G}(\operatorname{res}_{G, H}(\alpha)) = \lvert G : H\rvert \cdot \alpha\).

Multiplication by \(\lvert G\rvert\) annihilates \(H^n(G, M) = \operatorname{Ext}^n_{RG}(R, M)\) for every \(n > 0\). If \(\lvert G\rvert\) is invertible in \(R\) and \(M\) is an \(RG\)-module, then \(H^2(G, M) = 0\) so every extension of \(G\) by \(M\) splits, and \(H^1(G, M) = 0\) so all complements to \(M\) are conjugate by the classification of complements. Intuitively, \(\lvert G\rvert \cdot \alpha = \operatorname{Tr}_{\{1\}, G}(\operatorname{res}_{G, \{1\}}(\alpha))\) factors through \(\operatorname{Ext}^n_R(R, M{\downarrow_{\{1\}}})\), which is zero for \(n > 0\) because \(R\) is already projective over \(R\).

Central extensions by \(k^\times\) and twisted group rings. In a central extension of \(G\) by \(k^\times\), the infinite scalar group \(k^\times\) can be replaced by a finite cyclic subgroup of roots of unity whenever \(k\) has enough roots. Let \(\tilde{G}\) be a central extension of a finite group \(G\) by the multiplicative group \(k^\times\) of a field \(k\) in which every element has a \(\lvert G\rvert\)-th root. Then \(\tilde{G}\) contains a finite subgroup \(\hat{G}\) with \(\tilde{G} = \hat{G} \cdot k^\times\) and \(Z = \hat{G} \cap k^\times\) a cyclic group of order coprime to \(p = \operatorname{char}(k)\). In particular, if \(G\) is a \(p\)-group and \(k\) is a perfect field of characteristic \(p\) (a field in which every element has a \(p\)-th root, for example, every finite field), the extension splits and \(\tilde{G} = G \times k^\times\). Intuitively, multiplication by \(\lvert G\rvert\) kills \(H^2(G, k^\times)\) and every element of \(k^\times\) has a \(\lvert G\rvert\)-th root, so the coset representatives of \(G\) in \(\tilde{G}\) can be rescaled to make the \(2\)-cocycle \(\alpha[g_i \mid g_j]\) take values in the \(\lvert G\rvert\)-th roots of unity in \(k^\times\).

The hypothesis that every element of \(k\) has a \(\lvert G\rvert\)-th root cannot be dropped: for \(k = \mathbb{Q}\) and \(G = C_2\), the central extension \(\tilde{G} = \langle \mathbb{Q}^\times, \sqrt{2} \rangle \le \mathbb{R}^\times\) has no finite subgroup mapping onto \(G\) because \(\pm 1 \in \mathbb{Q}^\times\) are the only elements of finite order in \(\mathbb{R}^\times\). Given a \(2\)-cocycle \(\alpha : G \times G \to k^\times\), the twisted group ring \([kG]_\alpha\) is the \(k\)-algebra with basis \(\{\tilde{g}_i : g_i \in G\}\) and multiplication \(\tilde{g}_i \tilde{g}_j = \alpha[g_i \mid g_j]\widetilde{g_i g_j}\). When \(k\) is algebraically closed, choosing a finite central extension \(1 \to Z \to \hat{G} \to G \to 1\) as above with an inclusion \(Z \hookrightarrow k^\times\) identifies \([kG]_\alpha\) with the direct summand of \(k\hat{G}\) on which each \(z \in Z\) acts as the scalar \(z \in k^\times\) itself, so as a \(k\hat{G}\)-module \([kG]_\alpha \cong \varepsilon_Z{\uparrow^{\hat{G}}}\) is induced from the \(1\)-dimensional \(kZ\)-module \(\varepsilon_Z\) on which \(Z\) acts via \(Z \hookrightarrow k^\times\).

Lifting algebra automorphisms of \(\operatorname{End}_k(V)\). Suppose that a finite group \(G\) acts as \(k\)-algebra automorphisms on \(\operatorname{End}_k(V)\), where \(V\) is a finite-dimensional vector space over an algebraically closed field \(k\) of characteristic \(p\). Then a finite cyclic \(p'\)-central extension \(\hat{G}\) of \(G\), meaning a central extension of \(G\) by a finite cyclic group of order coprime to \(p\), acts linearly on \(V\) so that its induced conjugation action on \(V \otimes_k V^* \cong \operatorname{End}_k(V)\) is the given action of \(G\). By the Skolem–Noether theorem, every \(k\)-algebra automorphism of the matrix algebra \(\operatorname{End}_k(V)\) is conjugation by a matrix in \(\operatorname{GL}(V)\) unique up to a scalar in \(k^\times\), so the action of \(G\) pulls \(\operatorname{GL}(V)\) back to a central extension of \(G\) by \(k^\times\) to which the previous proposition applies.

Discrete valuation rings and \(p\)-adic integers. A discrete valuation ring is a principal ideal domain whose non-zero ideals are the powers \(\mathfrak{p}^i = (\pi^i)\) of a unique maximal ideal \(\mathfrak{p} = (\pi)\), generated by an element \(\pi\) called a uniformiser. It is a complete discrete valuation ring if every compatible sequence of residues modulo \(\pi, \pi^2, \pi^3, \dots\) comes from a single element of the ring, which is the property needed to pass from step-by-step lifts modulo \(\pi^i\) to an actual lift. The prototype is the ring of \(p\)-adic integers \(\mathbb{Z}_p\) for a prime \(p\), with uniformiser \(\pi = p\) and maximal ideal \(\mathfrak{p} = p\mathbb{Z}_p\): its elements are formal power series \(a_0 + a_1 p + a_2 p^2 + \cdots\) with digits \(a_i \in \{0, \dots, p - 1\}\), its quotients are \(\mathbb{Z}_p/p^i\mathbb{Z}_p \cong \mathbb{Z}/p^i\mathbb{Z}\), and its field of fractions is the field of \(p\)-adic numbers \(\mathbb{Q}_p = \mathbb{Z}_p[1/p]\).

\(p\)-modular systems. To connect modular representations in characteristic \(p\) with ordinary representations in characteristic \(0\), a \(p\)-modular system is a triple \((K, \mathcal{O}, k)\) where \(\mathcal{O}\) is a complete discrete valuation ring with maximal ideal \(\mathfrak{p}\), field of fractions \(K\) of characteristic \(0\), and residue field \(k = \mathcal{O}/\mathfrak{p}\) of characteristic \(p\) (such as \((\mathbb{Q}_p, \mathbb{Z}_p, \mathbb{F}_p)\)). Suppose a finitely generated \(kG\)-module \(M\) of dimension \(n\) has already been lifted to an \((\mathcal{O}/\mathfrak{p}^i)G\)-lattice \(M_i\). Lifting \(M_i\) one step further to \(\mathcal{O}/\mathfrak{p}^{i+1}\) means lifting the homomorphism \(G \to \operatorname{GL}_n(\mathcal{O}/\mathfrak{p}^i)\) across the group extension \(1 \to \operatorname{End}_k(M) \to \operatorname{GL}_n(\mathcal{O}/\mathfrak{p}^{i+1}) \to \operatorname{GL}_n(\mathcal{O}/\mathfrak{p}^i) \to 1\), whose obstruction lies in \(H^2(G, \operatorname{End}_k(M)) \cong \operatorname{Ext}^2_{kG}(M, M)\).

Green's lifting theorem. When \(\operatorname{Ext}^2_{kG}(M, M)\) vanishes, every step-by-step obstruction vanishes and \(M\) lifts all the way to \(\mathcal{O}\). Formally, suppose \((K, \mathcal{O}, k)\) is a \(p\)-modular system with \(k = \mathcal{O}/\mathfrak{p}\), and \(M\) is a finitely generated \(kG\)-module such that \(\operatorname{Ext}^2_{kG}(M, M) = 0\); then there exists an \(\mathcal{O}G\)-lattice \(\hat{M}\) with \(\hat{M}/\mathfrak{p}\hat{M} \cong M\).

Maranda's lifting theorem. When \(\operatorname{Ext}^2_{kG}(M, M) \neq 0\), a wrong lift at an early stage can get stuck later. For example, for \(i \ge 3\), the trivial \(\mathbb{F}_2 C_2\)-module lifts to the \(1 \times 1\) matrix \((2^{i-1} + 1)\) over \(\mathbb{Z}/2^i\mathbb{Z}\), which then fails to lift to \(\mathbb{Z}/2^{i+1}\mathbb{Z}\) because \((2^{i-1} + 1 + 2^i t)^2 \equiv 1 + 2^i \not\equiv 1 \pmod{2^{i+1}}\).

Once a lift reaches a high enough power of \(p\), however, its reduction modulo a slightly smaller power of \(p\) always lifts all the way to \(\mathcal{O}\). Suppose \(G\) is a finite group of order \(p^r q\) with \(q\) coprime to \(p\), and \((K, \mathcal{O}, k)\) is a \(p\)-modular system (where for \(\mathcal{O} = \mathbb{Z}_p\) the ideals \(p^a\mathcal{O}\) and \(\mathfrak{p}^a\) agree). If \(M\) is a finitely generated \(kG\)-module that lifts to a finitely generated \(\mathcal{O}/p^a\mathcal{O}\)-free \((\mathcal{O}/p^a\mathcal{O})G\)-module \(\tilde{M}\) with \(a \ge 2r + 1\), then there is a finitely generated \(\mathcal{O}\)-free \(\mathcal{O}G\)-module \(\hat{M}\) with \(\hat{M}/p^{a-r}\hat{M} \cong \tilde{M}/p^{a-r}\tilde{M}\). The obstruction at each stage is killed by \(p^r\), so by giving up \(r\) layers of precision one can always continue.

docs.title: Maths 3 - Projective Geometry
docs.text:
Projective geometry is a very significant area since it is effectively how human beings view the world. We see the 3D world as it is projected onto our retinas in 2D. Similarly, computer vision also projects the 3D world onto a 2D computer screen (or whatever else). Projective geometry is also important in physics, for example in the AdS/CFT formalism, where the bulk is projected onto the boundary.

Projective geometry should be quite intuitive on one level because it is essentially what is happening when you shine a torch at something, and a shadow falls on a wall or the floor. What is happening here is that rays of light are grazing the surface of the object i.e. they are tangential to the surface, and then go on to strike the surface serving as the projective wall or plane.

We will do much the same thing in a little while when we take a vector space of \((d+1)\)-dimensions, then send out rays/vectors from the origin, and take note of where they intersect a \(d\)-dimensional subspace that functions as our projective space. This place projective geometry under the umbrella of vector spaces and algebra.

But before that, we look at projective geometry axiomatically, which is called the synthetic approach, so that we understand projective geometry not just in terms of algebra, but also structurally and visually.

In the Euclidean plane that we are familiar with, \(\mathbb{R}^2\), we know that any two distinct lines are concurrent (i.e. they meet at a single point), unless they are parallel, and any two distinct points determine a single line. To eliminate the exception of parallelism and make the rule general, we work with the Extended Euclidean Plane (EEP), where we first define a pencil of lines (i.e. given a line, the pencil of lines associated with it are all lines parallel to it). We say that every pencil of lines meets at a distinct point at infinity. Since we require that any two distinct points determine a single line, we then say that all these distinct points at infinity are collinear and lie on the line at infinity called \(l_\infty\). If \(l\) is a line in the Euclidean plane, we denote \(l^*\) as the line in the EEP.

As a matter of notation, we define a triple \((P, L, I)\) to be a set \(P\) whose elements are called points, a set \(L\) of subsets of \(P\) whose elements are called lines (or blocks),and an incidence relation \(I\) which describes precisely which points belong to which lines (blocks).

For example, the Euclidean plane is a triple \((P, L, I)\), where \(P = \{(x, y) \mid x, y \in \mathbb{R}\}\), \(L = \{[a, b, c] \mid a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}, a, b \text{ not both zero}\}\); \(I\) : point \((x, y)\) lies on line \([a, b, c]\) if and only if \(ax + by + c = 0\).

It is sometimes convenient, particularly when \(P\) and \(L\) are finite sets, to express \(I\) as a subset of \(P \times L\). For example, consider the triple \((P, L, I)\) given by: \(P = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}\); \(L = \{a, b, c, d, e, f\}\); \(I = \{(1, a),(2, a),(3, b),(4, b),(1, c),(3, c),(2, d),(4, d),(1, e),(4, e),(2, f),(3, f)\}\).

This means that points \(1\) and \(2\) lie on line \(a\), points \(3\) and \(4\) lie on line \(b\), and so on.

In general, in projective geometry, we have The Principle of Duality. If \(T\) is a theorem valid in the EEP, and \(T'\) is the statement obtained from \(T\) by making the following changes: point \(\leftrightarrow\) line, collinear \(\leftrightarrow\) concurrent, join \(\leftrightarrow\) intersection, and whatever grammatical adjustments that are necessary, then \(T'\) (called the Dual Theorem) is a valid theorem in the EEP.

docs.title: Axioms of Projective Geometry
docs.text:
We can create a set of axioms that define the rules of an r-dimensional projective space. An \(r\)-dimensional projective space \(S_r\), \(r \ge 2\), is such that

A1. \(S_r\) is a set whose elements are called points.

A2. For every integer \(h\), with \(-1 \le h \le r\), there are subsets of \(S_r\), called subspaces of \(S_r\) of dimension \(h\). A subspace of \(S_r\) of dimension \(h\) is usually denoted by \(S_h\), and we write \(\dim S_h = h\).

A3. There is a unique subspace \(S_{-1}\) of \(S_r\) called the null subspace. (\(S_{-1}\) and \(S_r\) are called the non-proper subspaces, and all other subspaces are proper subspaces.)

A4. The points of \(S_r\) are the only subspaces of dimension \(0\).

A5. There is a unique subspace of dimension \(r\), namely \(S_r\).

A6. If \(S_h\) and \(S_k\) are two subspaces of \(S_r\), and \(S_h \subseteq S_k\), then \(h \le k\). Further, \(S_h = S_k\) if and only if \(h = k\).

A7. Given two subspaces \(S_h\) and \(S_k\) of \(S_r\), then \(S_h \cap S_k\) is a subspace \(S_i\) of \(S_r\).

A8. Given two subspaces \(S_h\) and \(S_k\) of \(S_r\), the span of \(S_h\) and \(S_k\), denoted by \(S_h \oplus S_k\) or by \(\langle S_h, S_k \rangle\), is the intersection of all the subspaces of \(S_r\) containing both \(S_h\) and \(S_k\). Let \(S_h \cap S_k = S_i\) and \(S_h \oplus S_k = S_c\). Then

\[h + k = i + c,\]

that is: \(\dim S_h + \dim S_k = \dim (S_h \cap S_k) + \dim (S_h \oplus S_k)\).

This is called the Grassmann Dimension Formula or Grassmann's Identity. We'll talk about this a little bit more soon.

A9. (Fano’s Postulate) Every \(S_1\) of \(S_r\) contains at least three points.

Now for some terminology. In an \(r\)-dimensional projective space \(S_r\) a one-dimensional subspace \(S_1\) is called a line. A two-dimensional subspace \(S_2\) is called a plane. A three-dimensional subspace \(S_3\) is called a solid. An \((r - 1)\)-dimensional subspace \(S_{r-1}\) is called a hyperplane of the \(S_r\). Points which lie on the same line are said to be collinear. Points or lines which lie on the same plane are said to be coplanar. Lines which pass through the same point are said to be concurrent.

We will see that every line in a projective space has the same number of points, say \(q+1\). The number \(q\) is called the order of the space.

docs.title: Projective Plane
docs.text:
A projective plane is a 2D projective space. We can take the axioms of an \(r\)-dimensional projective space and come up with something specific for a projective plane. The EEP is an example of a projective plane. Later, we will generalize the results for a projective space.

A projective plane \(\pi\) is a set \(P\) of points and a set \(L\) of subsets of \(P\), called lines, satisfying the following:

There exists a unique line joining two distinct points.

There exists a unique point of intersection of two distinct lines.

There exist at least three non-collinear points.

There exist at least three points on each line.

If \(\pi\) has a finite number \(N_2\) of points. Then:

Every line of \(\pi\) has the same number \(N_1 = q + 1\) of points. The order of the plane is \(q\).

The number \(N_2\) of points in \(\pi\) is \(q^2 + q + 1 = \frac{q^3 - 1}{q - 1}\).

By the principle of duality in the plane:

number of points on a line = number of lines through a point = \(q + 1\),

number of points in the plane = number of lines in the plane = \(q^2 + q + 1\).

Note that every finite projective plane of order 2 is a Fano Plane. In other words, the projective plane P has seven points and seven lines, and, with a suitable numbering 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 of the points, the lines of P are the point sets {1, 2, 3}, {1, 4, 5}, {1, 6, 7}, {2, 4, 7}, {2, 5, 6}, {3, 4, 6} and {3, 5, 7}.

Figure 1 draws this seven-point plane with the numbering above, highlighting point \(1\) with its three concurrent lines and line \(\{3, 4, 6\}\) with its three collinear points.

Figure 1. The Fano plane of order \(q = 2\), with \(N_2 = q^2 + q + 1 = 7\) points \(\{1, \dots, 7\}\) and \(7\) lines of \(N_1 = q + 1 = 3\) points each: the three sides \(\{2, 4, 7\}\), \(\{2, 5, 6\}\), \(\{3, 4, 6\}\), the three medians \(\{1, 2, 3\}\), \(\{1, 4, 5\}\), \(\{1, 6, 7\}\), and the seventh line \(\{3, 5, 7\}\). Point \(1\) lies on three concurrent lines (amber), and line \(\{3, 4, 6\}\) carries three collinear points (blue). Only the seven numbered nodes are points of the plane; \(\{3, 5, 7\}\) is drawn as a circle because no seven-point configuration of three-point lines can be drawn with straight segments alone in the Euclidean plane.

docs.title: \(r\)-dimensional Projective Space
docs.text:
More generally, if an \(r\)-dimensional projective space has a finite number \(N_r\) of points, then every line of \(S_r\) has the same number \(q+1\) of points. The number \(q\) is called the order of the space \(S_r\). \(N_r = q^r + q^{r-1} + \dots + q + 1 = \frac{q^{r+1} - 1}{q - 1}\). Note that the order is always defined based on the number of points on a line (and not a hyperplane or any other subspace), irrespective of the dimension of the projective space.

Duality associates points with hyperplanes, which are \((r-1)\)-dimensional projective subspaces of \(S_r\). In general, for all \(n\), with \(0 \le n \le r\), a subspace \(S_n\) of dimension \(n\) is dual to a subspace \(S_{r-n-1}\) of dimension \(r - n - 1\).

If \(U\) be a \(n\)-dimensional subspace of \(\mathbf{P}\) (\(1 \le n \le r\)) then \(U\) is itself a projective space and the number of points of \(U\) is:

\[q^n + q^{n-1} + \dots + q + 1 = \frac{q^{n+1} - 1}{q - 1}\]

The number of lines of \(U\) through a fixed point of \(U\) equals:

\[q^{n-1} + \dots + q + 1 = \frac{q^n - 1}{q - 1}\]

You can arrive at this by seeing that by duality this is the same number as the number of \((n-2)\)-D subspaces contained in an \((n-1)\)-subspace of \(U\). By duality once again, this is in turn the same as the number of points in a \((n-1)\)-subspace. Just for kicks, note that this number can also be arrived at by seeing that every line of \(U\) through \(P\) contains \(P\) plus \(q\) other points of \(U\), and every point \(Q \neq P\) lies on a unique line through \(P\). Dividing the remaining points by \(q\) points per line gives the number of lines through \(P\) (and by duality, the number of \((n-2)\)-subspaces in an \((n-1)\)-subspace): \(\frac{q(q^n - 1)}{q(q - 1)} = \frac{q^n - 1}{q - 1} = q^{n-1} + \dots + q + 1\)

Getting back to our original thread, the total number of lines of \(U\) equals:

\[\frac{(q^n + q^{n-1} + \dots + q + 1)(q^{n-1} + \dots + q + 1)}{q + 1} = \frac{(q^{n+1} - 1)(q^n - 1)}{(q^2 - 1)(q - 1)}\]

Note that all of these hold for \(\mathbf{P}\) also by setting \(n = r\).

docs.title: 3-dimensional Projective Space \(S_3\)
docs.text:
In the projective space \(S_3\) of dimension \(3\),

a point (of dimension \(0\)) is dual to a plane (of dimension \(2 = 3 - 0 - 1\)),

a line (of dimension \(1\)) is dual to a line (of dimension \(1 = 3 - 1 - 1\))

Number of points = \(q^3 + q^2 + q + 1\) = number of planes.

Number of planes containing a line \(\ell\) = number of points on a line \(\ell\) = \(q + 1\).

Number of lines through a point = number of lines in a plane = \(q^2 + q + 1\).

Though we have a formula derived above for this, counting the number of lines in the space in a few different ways helps to give an intuition of the kind of numbers and combinatorics encountered in projective spaces especially over finite fields.

Counting the number of lines in \(S_3\) - Method I: Let \(N\) be the number of lines in \(S_3\). We count the number \(M\) of pairs \((\ell, P)\), where \(P\) is a point lying on the line \(\ell\). On each of the \(N\) lines of \(S_3\) there are \(q + 1\) points. Thus,

\[M = N(q + 1).\]

Further, through each of the \(q^3 + q^2 + q + 1\) points of \(S_3\), there pass \(q^2 + q + 1\) lines. Therefore,

\[M = (q^2 + q + 1)(q^3 + q^2 + q + 1).\]

Hence

\[N = \frac{M}{q + 1} = \frac{(q^2 + q + 1)(q^3 + q^2 + q + 1)}{q + 1}\] \[= (q^2 + q + 1)(q^2 + 1)\] \[= q^4 + q^3 + 2q^2 + q + 1.\]

Counting the number of lines in \(S_3\) - Method II: Each pair of the \(q^3 + q^2 + q + 1\) points of \(S_3\) gives rise to a line, and any line is specified by a pair of its \(q + 1\) points, the number of lines of \(S_3\) is

\[N = \frac{\binom{q^3+q^2+q+1}{2}}{\binom{q+1}{2}}\] \[= \frac{(q^3 + q^2 + q + 1)(q^3 + q^2 + q)}{(q + 1)q}\] \[= \frac{(q^2 + 1)(q + 1)q(q^2 + q + 1)}{(q + 1)q}\] \[= (q^2 + 1)(q^2 + q + 1)\] \[= q^4 + q^3 + 2q^2 + q + 1.\]

docs.title: Grassman Formula for Intersection of Spaces
docs.text:
As we saw earlier, the Grassmann Dimension Formula or Grassmann's Identity relates the dimensions of two subspaces \(U\) and \(W\) to the dimensions of their intersection (meet) and their span (join). Because projective dimension is always \(1\) less than the underlying vector space dimension (we'll talk about this soon), the formula looks identical in both settings, provided you use the convention that the empty projective subspace \(\emptyset\) has projective dimension \(-1\).

For any two projective subspaces \(U\) and \(W\) in a projective space \(PG(n, \mathbb{F})\):

\[\dim(U) + \dim(W) = \dim(U \vee W) + \dim(U \cap W)\]

where: \(U \vee W\) (Join / Span) is the smallest projective subspace containing both \(U\) and \(W\). \(U \cap W\) (Meet / Intersection) is the largest projective subspace contained in both \(U\) and \(W\) (with \(\dim(\emptyset) = -1\) if \(U\) and \(W\) are disjoint/skew).

When looking at the dimensions of subspaces, there is a concept called codimension which makes it easy to see how different subspaces interact. If \(S \subset H\) and \(\dim S = M - c\), then it has codimension \(c\) inside \(H\). Let \(K \subset H\) have dimension \(k\). Apply the Grassmann formula to find a minimum dimension of their intersection (where the span of these two subspaces is set to a maximum of M):

\[\dim(S \cap K) \ge (M - c) + k - M = k - c\]

Remember that in projective geometry, the empty set has dimension \(\dim(\emptyset) = -1\), while a non-empty intersection (at least a point) requires \(\dim(S \cap K) \ge \mathbf{0}\). Therefore, an intersection is guaranteed if and only if:

\[k - c \ge 0 \iff \mathbf{k \ge c} \quad (\text{Dimension} \ge \text{Codimension})\]

Let's look at some examples. A \(\text{codim } c = 1\) subspace is forced to intersect a line \(K\) (\(\dim K = 1\)) because dimension \(1\) and codimension \(1\) "fill each other out" (their vector space dimensions are \(2\) and \(m\) inside an \((m+1)\)-dimensional vector space, summing to \(m + 2 > m + 1\)).

But \(\text{codim } c = 2\) will not be filled out by \(\dim k = 1\) (a line), leaving "wiggle room" for them to miss each other completely (just like two skew lines in \(PG(3, F)\), where a line has \(\dim 1\) but \(\text{codim } 3 - 1 = 2\)).

Again, \(\text{codim } c = 2\) and \(\dim k = 3\) will intersect in at least a \(1\)-dimensional line because \(k - c = 3 - 2 = \mathbf{1} \ge 0\).

docs.title: A Few Properties of Projective Subspaces
docs.text:
If \(\mathbf{P}\) be a projective space and \(U\) be a subspace of \(\mathbf{P}\), and \(p\) be a point of \(\mathbf{P}\) outside of \(U\). We have:

\[\langle U, p \rangle = \bigcup \{pu \mid u \in U\}\]

In other words, the subspace \(\langle U, p \rangle\) consists of the point \(p\) and all points \(z\) such that the line \(pz\) meets the subspace \(U\) in a point.

If \(B\) is a basis of \(U\), then \(B \cup p\) is unsurprisingly a basis of \(\langle U, p \rangle\). As a side note, if the number of basis elements is \(d+1\), the dimension of \(U\) is \(d\). The dimension of \(\langle U, p \rangle = d+1\).

Let \(U_1\) and \(U_2\) be two nonempty subspaces of a projective space \(\mathbf{P}\). Then the subspace \(\langle U_1, U_2 \rangle = \langle U_1 \cup U_2 \rangle\) generated by \(U_1\) and \(U_2\) is given directly by the union of all lines joining a point of \(U_1\) to a point of \(U_2\):

\[\langle U_1, U_2 \rangle = U_1 \cup U_2 \cup \bigcup \{u_1 u_2 \mid u_1 \in U_1,\, u_2 \in U_2,\, u_1 \neq u_2\}\]

If \(U_1\) and \(U_2\) are disjoint (\(U_1 \cap U_2 = \emptyset\)), this simplifies to the exact analogue of the single-point formula \(\langle U, p \rangle = \bigcup \{pu \mid u \in U\}\):

\[\langle U_1, U_2 \rangle = \bigcup \{u_1 u_2 \mid u_1 \in U_1,\, u_2 \in U_2\}\]

In other words, a point \(z \in \mathbf{P}\) lies in \(\langle U_1, U_2 \rangle\) if and only if \(z \in U_1 \cup U_2\) or there is a line through \(z\) that intersects both \(U_1\) and \(U_2\).

If \(\mathbf{P}\) is a projective space, \(U\) a subspace, and \(p\) a point not in \(U\), then as we saw, \(W = \langle U, p\rangle\) is a subspace of \(\mathbf{P}\). If we take a point \(q \neq p\) in \(W\), then \(W = \langle U, p\rangle = \langle U, q \rangle\). Nothing surprising here since for example, if you took a line and a point not on it, you would generate a plane with them. Take any other point on that plane and regenerate a new plane with the line and that new point. You end up with the same old plane!

Let \(\mathbf{P}\) be a projective space, and let \(U\) and \(W\) be two subspaces of \(\mathbf{P}\). \(U\) and \(W\) are called complementary if \(U \cap W = \emptyset\) and \(\langle U, W \rangle = \mathbf{P}\). In this case, if \(W\) is of finite dimension \(r\), \(U\) is called a subspace of codimension \(r + 1\). For example, a hyperplane has dimension \(d-1\), while a point is complementary to it and has dimension \(d=0\). We met this term "codimension" just a little while ago.

Let \(\mathbf{P}\) be a \(d\)-dimensional projective space, and let \(U\) and \(W\) be two subspaces of \(\mathbf{P}\) with \(U \cap W = \emptyset\). Then, there exists a subspace \(W'\) through \(W\) such that \(U\) and \(W'\) are complementary. Note that \(W'\) through \(W\) implies that \(W'\) contains \(W\). Once we have that clarity, this proposition is obvious. If \(U\) and \(W\) are complementary then any \(W'\) that \(W\) is a subspace of must intersect \(U\) by the Grassmann formula and the dimension/codimension analysis we did earlier.

docs.title: Vector Spaces and Projective Geometry
docs.text:
Purely axiomatic geometry (also called synthetic geometry) lacks a coordinate system, making it very difficult to compute transformations, intersections, or specific loci. We want to label these abstract points and lines with coordinates so we can calculate with them and get geometrical results by mechanically manipulating numbers.

Before going further, we must point out that every axiomatic projective space of dimension greater than or equal to 3 can be constructed out of a \((d+1)\)-dimensional vector space \(V\) over some division ring (which includes skew fields) \(K\). Note that a skew field ring is almost the same as a field, except that multiplication must commute in a field, but need not in a division ring. Inverses still commute and are unique.

If dimension \(d = 2\) i.e. if we are looking at projective planes, then we may not be able to find such vector spaces for certain projective planes called non-Desarguesian planes. Essentially, they cannot be embedded inside any 3D projective space. We will not bother about such planes here, but one important plane is the Moufang / Octonion Plane \(\mathbb{O}\mathbb{P}^2\), which is built using the 8-dimensional Octonions \(\mathbb{O}\), where multiplication is non-associative. Because octonions are not associative, you cannot form a true vector space over them, and \(\mathbb{O}\mathbb{P}^2\) cannot exist inside any \(\mathbb{O}\mathbb{P}^3\).

To make the geometry of a projective space calculable, we construct a \(d\)-dimensional projective space out of a standard \((d+1)\)-dimensional vector space \(V\) over a field \(\mathbb{F}\) (such as \(\mathbb{F}^3\) for a 2D projective plane). By intentionally defining projective objects as vector subspaces, the geometry inherits the robust machinery of linear algebra.

Think of it this way. Take a 3D vector space. Draw a vector from the origin. This vector will pierce the \(z=1\) plane at a point. This point represents a point on the projective plane. Of course, the vector will pierce every plane \(z = k \in \mathbf{C}\) except the \(z=0\) plane. All these points are considered an equivalence class, which is no different from saying the \(1D\) vector is equivalent to the projective point. The points at infinity are formed by the intersection of vectors with the \(z=0\) plane at infinity. Thus:

A Projective Point is defined as a 1-dimensional vector subspace (a line extending through the origin in \(V\)). A Projective Line is defined as a 2-dimensional vector subspace (a plane extending through the origin in \(V\)). The Projective Plane (dimension \(2\)) is defined as the entire \(3\)D vector space \(V = \mathbb{F}^3\). The "\(-1\) relationship in dimensions continues into higher dimensions.

This algebraic translation automatically satisfies the abstract axioms. For instance, the axiom stating "any two projective lines must intersect in exactly one projective point" simply becomes the standard linear algebra theorem: "In a 3-dimensional vector space, the intersection of any two distinct 2-dimensional subspaces must be a 1-dimensional subspace."

However, once again, as we saw earlier, we end up rules with qualifications. For example, two lines meet at a point - unless they are parallel. Another example: the intersection of \(a_1x + b_1y = c_1\) and \(a_2x + b_2y = c_2\) is found by Cramer's rule... unless the determinant is zero. A third example: a conic section can be an ellipse, a parabola, or a hyperbola... depending on how its asymptotes behave.

To avoid these qualifications, we saw how to add points at infinity where parallel lines meet. Similarly, conics stop having three different names: parabolas and hyperbolas are simply ellipses that happen to touch or cross at a point at infinity.

To label all these points, we use something like the usual coordinate system of \((x, y)\) but add an additional \(z\) coordinate such that the coordinates of the points on the line at infinity have \(z=0\), while the other points are \(z=1\). Of course, this leaves us in a bit of a quandary. What do the points with \(z \neq 0, 1\) mean? We need to map these back to the affine plane somehow. The trick that is used is to simply normalize \((x, y, z)\) by \(z\), so that \((\rho x, \rho y, \rho z)\) is the same as \((x, y, z)\). The ratio \(X/Z\) and \(Y/Z\) determines the point of the affine plane, and there is a whole equivalence class of coordinates in the projective plane, which differ only by the scale factor, that map to the same affine and projective plane point. For example, the equivalence class containing \((2, 4, 2)\) can be scaled by \(1/2\) to become \((1, 2, 1)\). This class represents the specific finite affine point \((1, 2)\).

When \(z=0\), the \(x\) and \(y\) values capture the direction vector of a line. Once again, for example because \((4, 8, 0) = 2 \cdot (2, 4, 0)\), both triples belong to the same equivalence class. Geometrically, this makes sense: a direction vector from the origin to \((2, 4)\) points in the exact same direction (a slope of \(2\)) as a direction vector from the origin to \((4, 8)\). Therefore, they define the exact same point on the line at infinity. Note that these coordinates, called homogenous coordinates are not something new. They are just the coordinate values of each basis vector that is needed to describe a vector of the \(d+1\)-dimensional vector space. Essentially, if we fix a basis \(\{v_0, v_1, \dots, v_d\}\) of \(V\). Then we can express any vector as \(v = a_0 v_0 + a_1 v_1 + \dots + a_d v_d \in V\) uniquely by its coordinates \((a_0, a_1, \dots, a_d)\) in that basis. Two homogenous coordinates \(a\) and \(b\) are an equivalence class and therefore the same point (as discussed above) if there is an \(\alpha \in F \setminus \{0\}\) such that \((a_0, a_1, \dots, a_d) = \alpha \cdot (b_0, b_1, \dots, b_d)\)

The vector space model directly reproduces the axiomatic count \(q^2 + q + 1\). The ambient vector space \(V = \mathbb{F}_q^3\) has \(q^3\) total vectors. Remove the origin \(\mathbf{0}\): \(q^3 - 1\) non-zero vectors. Every \(1\)-dimensional vector subspace contains \(q - 1\) non-zero scalar multiples of its spanning (unit) vector. The total number of \(1\)-dimensional subspaces (projective points) is: \(\frac{q^3 - 1}{q - 1} = q^2 + q + 1\).

By mapping the projective plane to subspaces of \(\mathbb{F}^3\), geometry instantly inherits the computational tools of linear algebra:

Finding the line through two points \(\mathbf{p}_1, \mathbf{p}_2\): Take the vector cross product: \(\boldsymbol{\ell} = \mathbf{p}_1 \times \mathbf{p}_2\)

Finding the intersection of two lines \(\boldsymbol{\ell}_1, \boldsymbol{\ell}_2\): Take the exact same cross product: \(\mathbf{p} = \boldsymbol{\ell}_1 \times \boldsymbol{\ell}_2\)

Checking if a point \(\mathbf{p} = (x, y, z)\) lies on a line \(\boldsymbol{\ell} = [a, b, c]\): Take the standard dot product: \(\boldsymbol{\ell} \cdot \mathbf{p} = ax + by + cz = 0\)

Checking collinearity of three points: Compute a single \(3 \times 3\) determinant: \(\det \begin{pmatrix} x_1 & y_1 & z_1 \\ x_2 & y_2 & z_2 \\ x_3 & y_3 & z_3 \end{pmatrix} = 0\)

Geometric problems become straightforward matrix and vector calculations. These rules generalize to higher dimensions \(PG(n, \mathbb{F})\) where the 3D cross product is replaced by the exterior wedge product (\(\wedge\)) and Plücker coordinates, which we won't immediately bother about right now. Similarly, in higher dimensions, we can use the dot product rule to check incidence of a point with a hyperplane. To check incidence between a point and a line or non-hyperplanes, we must take multiple dot products between the point and each additional linear constraint equation.

The vector space representation also includes the principle of duality. For example, because a point is a 1D subspace of \(\mathbb{F}^3\) and a line is a 2D subspace of \(\mathbb{F}^3\), the incidence condition:

\[ax + by + cz = 0\]

is completely symmetric between the point coordinates \((x, y, z)\) and the line coordinates \([a, b, c]\).

In linear algebra over a 3D vector space, a 2D subspace (a plane through the origin) is uniquely defined by its 1D normal vector (an element of the dual space \(V^*\)). This means every theorem true for points and lines is automatically true if you swap the words "point" and "line". You prove a theorem once, and you get its dual theorem for free without any additional work.

Note that these relations hold in higher dimensions as well between points and hyperplanes. Also, we have assumed that we are operating with left vector spaces, which is a fancy way of saying that we are using row vectors for the homogenous coordinates of points, and when we want to transform a row vector with a matrix, we do \(v.M\) (not \(M.v\)). With right vector spaces, this flips.

Additionally, the coordinates of a line/hyperplane may be written as \([a, b, c... ]\), but we actually mean a column vector \([a, b, c... ]^T\). Thus, the test for incidence being a dot product makes more sense now. It is simply \((x, y, z...)\cdot[a, b, c... ]^T\).

Thus, a hyperplane is always defined by a linear equation, \(x_0 a_0 + \dots + x_d a_d = 0\), which is pretty much what we see with a line on a plane. The homogenous coordinates of any point on this hyperplane satisify this equation. If however, we want to find the unique hyperplane passing through \(d\) points, we plug the coordinates of the \(d\) points into the hyperplane equation:
