Our quotient hierarchy and Ronan's theorem now tell us two further things about this quadric embedding. First, Ronan's theorem gives the grid an absolutely universal embedding, and the quadric embedding is isomorphic to a quotient of it. That quotient cannot be proper: a proper quotient induces strictly fewer hyperplanes than the embedding it comes from, and the quadric embedding already induces all \(15\). So \(\tilde{\epsilon} : Q^+(3, 2) \to \mathrm{PG}(3, 2)\) is itself the absolutely universal embedding of the grid. Second, \(\tilde{\epsilon}\) has no proper quotients: projecting \(\mathrm{PG}(3, 2)\) from a point, a line or a plane gives the \(7\)-point Fano plane \(\mathrm{PG}(2, 2)\), a \(3\)-point line or a single point, and none of these can receive \(9\) points injectively (equivalently, every one of the \(15 - 9 = 6\) points of \(\mathrm{PG}(3, 2)\) outside \(Q^+(3, 2)\) lies on secant lines joining noncollinear pairs of grid points). Thus the quadric embedding in \(\mathrm{PG}(3, 2)\) is the unique full projective embedding of \(Q^+(3, 2)\) up to isomorphism.

docs.title: The affine plane AG(2, 3): three points per line, zero hyperplanes, no embedding
docs.text:
Finally recall the affine plane \(\mathrm{AG}(2, 3)\) over \(\mathbb{F}_3\) (Figure 8(a)), the Steiner triple system \(S(2, 3, 9)\) with \(9\) points and \(12\) lines of \(3\) points obtained by deleting one line at infinity from \(\mathrm{PG}(2, 3)\).

It is tempting to object that \(\mathrm{AG}(2, 3)\) already sits inside the projective plane \(\mathrm{PG}(2, 3)\). Check the line sizes, though: every projective line of \(\mathrm{PG}(2, 3)\) has \(4\) points, whereas each affine line of \(\mathrm{AG}(2, 3)\) has only \(3\) points. Including \(\mathrm{AG}(2, 3)\) into \(\mathrm{PG}(2, 3)\) maps each affine line into three of the four points of a projective line rather than onto the full line, so it is not a full projective embedding.

Could \(\mathrm{AG}(2, 3)\) have a full projective embedding into some other projective space (which would have to be over \(\mathbb{F}_2\), since its lines have size \(3\))? Use Ronan's theorem and search for a hyperplane \(H \subsetneq \mathcal{P}\) of \(\mathrm{AG}(2, 3)\), meaning a proper subset meeting each of the \(12\) affine lines in \(1\) or \(3\) points (Figure 16). Clearly \(H\) cannot be empty, since \(\lvert \emptyset \cap L vert = 0\). Pick a point \(p \in H\) (Figure 16(a)). The \(4\) lines of \(\mathrm{AG}(2, 3)\) passing through \(p\) partition the remaining \(8\) points of \(\mathcal{P} \setminus \{p\}\). On each of those \(4\) lines, \(p\) is already in \(H\), so \(\lvert H \cap L vert \in \{1, 3\}\) leaves either \(0\) or \(2\) additional points of \(H\) on that line (an even number). Adding those four even counts to \(p\) itself shows that \(\lvert H vert\) must be odd. Now pick a point \(q otin H\), which exists because \(H eq \mathcal{P}\) (Figure 16(b)). The \(4\) lines of \(\mathrm{AG}(2, 3)\) through \(q\) partition \(\mathcal{P} \setminus \{q\}\), and on each of those \(4\) lines, having \(q otin H\) rules out \(\lvert H \cap L vert = 3\) and forces \(\lvert H \cap L vert = 1\). Summing across the \(4\) lines through \(q\) gives \(\lvert H vert = 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4\), which is even. No set can have size equal to \(4\) and odd at the same time, so \(\mathrm{AG}(2, 3)\) has zero hyperplanes and, by Ronan's theorem, no full projective embedding at all.

Figure 16. Why \(\mathrm{AG}(2, 3)\) has no hyperplanes (and hence, by Ronan's theorem, no full projective embedding). (a) The \(4\) affine lines through any point \(p \in H\) partition the other \(8\) points into \(4\) pairs; since \(\lvert H \cap L_i vert \in \{1, 3\}\), each pair contributes \(0\) or \(2\) points to \(H\), so \(\lvert H vert = 1 + ext{even}\) must be odd. (b) The \(4\) affine lines through any point \(q otin H\) also partition the other \(8\) points into \(4\) pairs; since \(q otin H\), each line must meet \(H\) in \(1\) point, forcing \(\lvert H vert = 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4\) (even), a contradiction.

Geometry \(\mathcal{S}\) Size Hyperplanes Full embeddings \(3\)-vane fan \(7\) pts, \(3\) lines \(15\) \(\mathrm{PG}(3, 2)\) (\(\lvert \mathcal{H}_{ ilde{\epsilon}} vert = 15\)); quotient \(\mathrm{PG}(2, 2)\) (\(\lvert \mathcal{H}_{ ilde{\epsilon}/\alpha} vert = 7\)) Grid \(Q^+(3, 2)\) \(9\) pts, \(6\) lines \(15\) \(\mathrm{PG}(3, 2)\) (\(\lvert \mathcal{H}_{ ilde{\epsilon}} vert = 15\)); no proper quotients \(\mathrm{AG}(2, 3)\) \(9\) pts, \(12\) lines \(0\) None

docs.title: Generalized Polygons
docs.text: We have already met projective planes (\(n = 3\)), generalized quadrangles (\(n = 4\)), and Jacques Tits's unified definition of generalized \(n\)-gons through ordinary \(n\)-gon subgeometries, along with the statement of the Feit–Higman theorem restricting finite thick generalized \(n\)-gons (\(n \ge 3\)) to \(n \in \{3, 4, 6, 8\}\). Two central questions remain open from that overview. First, how do three qualitative axioms about ordinary \(n\)-gon subgeometries force such rigid global structure, including unique shortest paths below the diameter, equal degrees for opposite elements, uniform orders \((s, t)\) for all thick polygons, and three equivalent ways to recognize a generalized polygon? Second, how does the distance-regular algebra of the collinearity graph rule out every finite thick generalized \(n\)-gon outside \(n \in \{2, 3, 4, 6, 8\}\)?

docs.title: Recalling the polygon axioms
docs.text:
Recall from our earlier overview of generalized polygons that a generalized \(2\)-gon (or generalized digon) has \(\lvert \mathcal{P} \rvert, \lvert \mathcal{L} \rvert \ge 2\) with every point incident with every line (\(I = \mathcal{P} \times \mathcal{L}\)), while for \(n \ge 3\) a generalized \(n\)-gon is a partial linear space \(\mathcal{S} = (\mathcal{P}, \mathcal{L}, I)\) satisfying three axioms on its ordinary \(m\)-gon subgeometries, which we label (GP1)–(GP3):

  • (GP1) \(\mathcal{S}\) has no subgeometries that are ordinary \(m\)-gons for any \(m \in \{3, 4, \dots, n - 1\}\) (vacuous when \(n = 3\));
  • (GP2) \(\mathcal{S}\) has subgeometries that are ordinary \(n\)-gons;
  • (GP3) for every pair \(\{A_1, A_2\} \subseteq \mathcal{P} \cup \mathcal{L}\) (two points, two lines, or a point and a line), there is a subgeometry \(\mathcal{S}' = (\mathcal{P}', \mathcal{L}', I')\) of \(\mathcal{S}\) isomorphic to an ordinary \(n\)-gon with \(\{A_1, A_2\} \subseteq \mathcal{P}' \cup \mathcal{L}'\).

Notice why (GP1)–(GP3) ask for ordinary \(n\)-gon subgeometries rather than full subgeometries: in the Fano plane \(\mathrm{PG}(2, 2)\), every line has \(3\) points, whereas each side of an ordinary triangle has only \(2\) points, so a triangle inside \(\mathrm{PG}(2, 2)\) keeps \(3\) noncollinear points and their \(3\) joining lines while dropping the third point on each line. As noted in our earlier overview, the point-line dual \(\mathcal{S}^D\) of any generalized \(n\)-gon is again a generalized \(n\)-gon, every ordinary \(n\)-gon (\(n \ge 3\)) is a generalized \(n\)-gon of order \((1, 1)\), and grids and dual grids are examples of generalized \(4\)-gons.

docs.title: Small-n equivalences and reconstructing a polygon from its collinearity graph
docs.text:
As stated earlier, for \(n = 3\) and \(n = 4\) the axioms (GP1)–(GP3) reduce to familiar incidence rules. Let us check both directions of those two equivalences, and then see why \(n \ge 4\) allows the geometry to be rebuilt from its collinearity graph alone.

Generalized \(3\)-gons and projective planes. The generalized \(3\)-gons are the possibly degenerate projective planes (both nondegenerate projective planes and near-pencils).

In one direction, suppose \(\mathcal{S} = (\mathcal{P}, \mathcal{L}, I)\) is a possibly degenerate projective plane, meaning a linear space in which any two distinct lines meet in a point and three noncollinear points exist. Then (GP1) holds vacuously, three noncollinear points with their three joining lines form an ordinary \(3\)-gon subgeometry for (GP2), and any two elements \(A_1, A_2 \in \mathcal{P} \cup \mathcal{L}\) can be completed to a triangle of three noncollinear points and their three joining lines for (GP3). Conversely, suppose \(\mathcal{S}\) is a generalized \(3\)-gon. By (GP2), \(\mathcal{S}\) contains an ordinary \(3\)-gon subgeometry, which supplies three noncollinear points. Given any two distinct points \(x_1, x_2 \in \mathcal{P}\), (GP3) places them inside a triangle, so they lie on a common line and \(\mathcal{S}\) is a linear space. Given any two distinct lines \(L_1, L_2 \in \mathcal{L}\), (GP3) places them inside a triangle, so they intersect in a point and \(\mathcal{S}\) is a possibly degenerate projective plane.

Generalized \(4\)-gons and generalized quadrangles. A partial linear space \(\mathcal{S} = (\mathcal{P}, \mathcal{L}, I)\) is a generalized \(4\)-gon if and only if it is a generalized quadrangle, meaning (GQ1) there exist two disjoint lines and (GQ2) for every anti-flag \((x, L)\), there is a unique point on \(L\) collinear with \(x\).

Suppose first that \(\mathcal{S}\) is a generalized \(4\)-gon satisfying (GP1)–(GP3) for \(n = 4\). Given an anti-flag \((x, L)\), (GP3) places \(x\) and \(L\) inside an ordinary \(4\)-gon subgeometry, which provides a point on \(L\) collinear with \(x\); if \(L\) contained two distinct points collinear with \(x\), then \(x\) and those two points together with \(L\) and the two joining lines from \(x\) would form an ordinary \(3\)-gon subgeometry, violating (GP1). Thus (GQ2) holds. To get (GQ1), take an ordinary \(4\)-gon subgeometry with opposite lines \(L_1, L_2\) and connecting lines \(L_3, L_4\); the lines \(L_1\) and \(L_2\) must be disjoint in \(\mathcal{S}\), because an intersection point would be collinear with both endpoints of \(L_3\), violating (GQ2).

Conversely, suppose \(\mathcal{S}\) is a partial linear space satisfying (GQ1) and (GQ2), with disjoint lines \(L_1\) and \(L_2\). As we verified when introducing generalized quadrangles, (GQ1) and (GQ2) force every point \(x\) of \(\mathcal{S}\) to lie on at least two lines: if \(x \in L_i\), then \(x\) lies on \(L_i\) and the unique line through \(x\) meeting \(L_{3-i}\); if \(x \notin L_1 \cup L_2\) and the unique lines \(M_1, M_2\) from \(x\) to \(L_1, L_2\) happen to coincide as one line \(M\) meeting \(L_1\) at \(u\) and \(L_2\) at \(v\), picking a second point \(u' \in L_1 \setminus \{u\}\) and joining it to its unique collinear partner \(v' \in L_2\) creates a line \(M' = u'v'\) disjoint from \(M\) (meeting \(M\) would give two points \(u, u'\) on \(L_1\) collinear with the intersection point), and projecting \(x\) onto \(M'\) gives a second line \(M'' \neq M\) through \(x\). By (GQ2), \(\mathcal{S}\) contains no ordinary \(3\)-gons, and because every point lies on at least two lines, (GQ2) lets us complete any pair \(A_1, A_2 \in \mathcal{P} \cup \mathcal{L}\) to an ordinary \(4\)-gon subgeometry.

Collinearity-graph reconstruction for \(n \ge 4\). Recall that the collinearity graph \(\Gamma\) of \(\mathcal{S}\) takes the point set \(\mathcal{P}\) as its vertex set, with two distinct points adjacent whenever they are collinear. When \(n = 3\), passing from \(\mathcal{S}\) to \(\Gamma\) loses all line structure: in any projective plane of order \(q\), every pair of points is collinear, so \(\Gamma\) is the complete graph \(K_{q^2+q+1}\) regardless of how the lines are wired. When \(n \ge 4\), however, (GP1) forbids ordinary \(3\)-gon subgeometries. That means three mutually collinear points can never sit on three distinct lines; any set of mutually collinear points must lie on a single line of \(\mathcal{S}\). Identifying each line with the set of points incident with it, every line of \(\mathcal{S}\) is a clique of \(\Gamma\), and because no point outside a line \(L\) can be collinear with more than one point of \(L\) (which has at least two points), the lines of \(\mathcal{S}\) are the maximal cliques of \(\Gamma\).

Reconstructing a generalized polygon from its collinearity graph. Let \(\mathcal{S}_1\) be a generalized \(n_1\)-gon and \(\mathcal{S}_2\) be a generalized \(n_2\)-gon with \(n_1, n_2 \ge 4\), and let \(\Gamma_1\) and \(\Gamma_2\) be their collinearity graphs. Then \(\mathcal{S}_1 \cong \mathcal{S}_2\) if and only if \(\Gamma_1 \cong \Gamma_2\).

Clearly \(\mathcal{S}_1 \cong \mathcal{S}_2\) implies \(\Gamma_1 \cong \Gamma_2\). Conversely, if \(\Gamma_1 \cong \Gamma_2\), then both \(\mathcal{S}_1\) and \(\mathcal{S}_2\) are isomorphic to the point-line geometry whose points are the vertices of \(\Gamma_1\) and whose lines are the maximal cliques of \(\Gamma_1\), with containment as incidence (which also forces \(n_1 = n_2\)).

docs.title: Basic properties of generalized polygons
docs.text:
A most useful thing to realize about a generalized polygon is that for any point \(y\) at distance \(i\) from another point \(x\), with \(1 \le i < \lfloor \frac{n}{2} \rfloor\), there is 1 unique road (\(L_{\text{in}}\)) leading back toward \(x\) (with 1 point \(z\) on that road at distance \(i - 1\), and \(s - 1\) fellow points on that road at distance \(i\)), and \(t\) roads leading strictly further away from \(x\) (where all \(s\) other points on each of those \(t\) roads are at distance \(i + 1\)). Figure 19(a) draws these layers.

More elaborately, there is only one shortest path (geodesic) between \(x\) and \(y\). There is no way to branch off from \(y\) and still reach \(x\) in \(i\) steps because among the \(t + 1\) lines passing through \(y\), only one line (\(L_{\text{in}}\)) heads back toward \(x\). The other \(t\) lines all head strictly away from \(x\).

The last layer \(i = \lfloor \frac{n}{2} \rfloor\) behaves differently, because there is no further layer to step out to. When \(n\) is even, all \(t + 1\) lines through \(y\) head back toward \(x\), each containing one point at distance \(i - 1\). When \(n\) is odd, one line still heads back, but the points on the other \(t\) lines stay at the same distance \(i\) from \(x\).

We will look at these points below.

docs.title: Incidence-graph axioms, geodesics, and diameter
docs.text:
To track paths and cycles cleanly, we use both graphs attached to \(\mathcal{S} = (\mathcal{P}, \mathcal{L}, I)\): the collinearity graph \(\Gamma\) on \(\mathcal{P}\), and the bipartite incidence graph \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) on \(\mathcal{P} \cup \mathcal{L}\) whose edges are the flags \(\{x, L\}\). As in the earlier notes, we write \(d(\cdot, \cdot)\) for distance in \(\Gamma\) (with distance spheres \(\Gamma_i(x)\), \(d(x, L) = \min_{y \in L} d(x, y)\), and \(d(L_1, L_2) = \min_{y_1 \in L_1, y_2 \in L_2} d(y_1, y_2)\)) and \(\delta(\cdot, \cdot)\) for distance in \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) (with distance spheres \(\widetilde{\Gamma}_i(x)\)), linked in any connected geometry by

\[\delta(x, y) = 2\,d(x, y), \qquad \delta(x, L) = 2\,d(x, L) + 1, \qquad \delta(L_1, L_2) = 2\,d(L_1, L_2) + 2\]

for all \(x, y \in \mathcal{P}\) and distinct \(L, L_1, L_2 \in \mathcal{L}\).

In any partial linear space \(\mathcal{S}\), a \(2m\)-cycle \(p_1, L_1, p_2, L_2, \dots, p_m, L_m, p_1\) in \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) (\(m \ge 3\)) alternates between \(m\) distinct points and \(m\) distinct lines, so \(2m\)-cycles of \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) correspond one-to-one with ordinary \(m\)-gon subgeometries of \(\mathcal{S}\) (and \(4\)-cycles cannot occur because two distinct points share at most one line). For any \(n \ge 3\), a partial linear space \(\mathcal{S}\) is therefore a generalized \(n\)-gon if and only if its incidence graph \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) satisfies three properties:

  • (GP1') \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) has no cycles of length \(2m\) for any \(m \in \{3, 4, \dots, n - 1\}\);
  • (GP2') \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) has a cycle of length \(2n\) (together, (GP1') and (GP2') say that \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) has girth \(2n\));
  • (GP3') every two vertices of \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) lie in a common cycle of length \(2n\).

Panel (a) of Figure 17 revisits \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) for the Fano plane (\(n = 3\)), the \(14\)-vertex Heawood graph of girth \(2n = 6\) and diameter \(n = 3\) that we first met in Figure 5(b), now highlighting an ordinary triangle subgeometry as a red \(6\)-cycle \((p_1, L_1, p_2, L_2, p_3, L_3)\) and showing how doubling subdivides each flag edge \(\{p_i, L_j\}\) with a new vertex. Throughout the rest of this section, let \(\mathcal{S}\) be a generalized \(n\)-gon with \(n \ge 3\). Because \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) has girth \(2n\), no cycle can be shorter than \(2n\), and that single fact governs all shortest paths and the diameter in both \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) and \(\Gamma\) (proving in particular the diameter formula \(\lfloor n / 2 floor\) stated earlier).

Figure 17. Geodesics, doubling, and vertex degrees in the incidence graph \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) of a generalized \(n\)-gon. (a) On the \(14\)-vertex Heawood graph \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) of \(\mathrm{PG}(2, 2)\) (\(n = 3\), diameter \(3\), girth \(6\), cf. Figure 5(b)), an ordinary \(3\)-gon subgeometry appears as a red \(6\)-cycle \((p_1, L_1, p_2, L_2, p_3, L_3)\), opposite vertices such as \(p_1\) and \(L_4\) lie at distance \(\delta(p_1, L_4) = 3 = n\), and doubling \(\mathrm{PG}(2, 2)\) inserts a flag vertex (orange diamond) on every edge to form a generalized \(6\)-gon of girth \(12\). (b) Top: unique geodesics of length \(n - 2\) pair the neighbours of opposite vertices \(x, y\) (\(\delta(x, y) = n\)) bijectively, so \(\deg(x) = \deg(y)\) (and \(s = t\) when \(n\) is odd). Bottom: when every vertex has degree at least \(3\), a third branch \(uz\) at the common neighbour \(u\) of \(x\) and \(y\) extends to a vertex \(v\) at distance \(n\) from both, forcing \(\deg(x) = \deg(v) = \deg(y)\) and a uniform order \((s, t)\).

Geodesics and diameter in the incidence graph \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\). In the incidence graph \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) of a generalized \(n\)-gon (\(n \ge 3\)):

  • (a) Any two vertices \(x\) and \(y\) of \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) at distance \(i = \delta(x, y) < n\) are joined by a unique shortest path.
  • (b) Whenever \(1 \le i = \delta(x, y) \le n - 1\), there is a unique neighbour of \(y\) at distance \(i - 1\) from \(x\), so \(\lvert \widetilde{\Gamma}_{i-1}(x) \cap \widetilde{\Gamma}_1(y) vert = 1\).
  • (c) If \(x_0, x_1, \dots, x_k\) is any walk in \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) of length \(k \le n\) that never steps straight back to the vertex it just left (\(x_{r-1} eq x_{r+1}\) for all \(1 \le r \le k - 1\)), then \(\delta(x_0, x_k) = k\).
  • (d) The diameter of \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) is equal to \(n\).

Let us verify (a)–(d) in order. For (a), if \(x\) and \(y\) had two different shortest paths of length \(i < n\), walking from \(x\) to \(y\) along the first path and returning along the second would trace a closed walk of length \(2i < 2n\) containing at least one simple cycle of length at most \(2i < 2n\), contradicting girth \(2n\). Claim (b) follows immediately from (a), because every vertex \(u \in \widetilde{\Gamma}_{i-1}(x) \cap \widetilde{\Gamma}_1(y)\) extends a shortest path of length \(i - 1\) from \(x\) to \(u\) by the edge \(uy\) into a shortest path of length \(i\) from \(x\) to \(y\).

For (c), suppose for contradiction that \(\delta(x_0, x_k) < k\), and let \(j\) be the largest index in \(\{0, 1, \dots, k\}\) satisfying \(\delta(x_0, x_j) = j\). Because \(\delta(x_0, x_0) = 0\) and \(\delta(x_0, x_1) = 1\) while \(\delta(x_0, x_k) < k\), we have \(1 \le j \le k - 1\). What is \(\delta(x_0, x_{j+1})\)? By the triangle inequality it is at most \(j + 1\); by the maximality of \(j\) it cannot equal \(j + 1\); and because \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) is bipartite, the adjacent vertices \(x_j\) and \(x_{j+1}\) cannot lie at the same distance \(j\) from \(x_0\). Thus \(\delta(x_0, x_{j+1}) = j - 1\). That puts both \(x_{j-1}\) and \(x_{j+1}\) into \(\widetilde{\Gamma}_{j-1}(x_0) \cap \widetilde{\Gamma}_1(x_j)\), and since the walk does not backtrack (\(x_{j-1} eq x_{j+1}\)), \(x_j\) has two distinct neighbours at distance \(j - 1\) from \(x_0\), contradicting (b).

For (d), (GP3') places any two vertices of \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) inside a \(2n\)-cycle, so their distance is at most half the cycle length, giving \(\operatorname{diam}(\widetilde{\Gamma}) \le n\). Conversely, walking \(n\) steps along one half of a \(2n\)-cycle gives a non-backtracking walk \(x_0, x_1, \dots, x_n\), which achieves \(\delta(x_0, x_n) = n\) by (c).

Translating (a)–(d) from \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) to \(\Gamma\) via \(\delta(x, y) = 2\,d(x, y)\) gives the matching rules in the collinearity graph:

Property (\(n \ge 3\)) In the incidence graph \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) (distance \(\delta\)) In the collinearity graph \(\Gamma\) (distance \(d\)) Unique shortest path For \(\delta(x, y) = i < n\), a unique shortest path joins \(x\) and \(y\) For \(d(x, y) \le \lfloor rac{n-1}{2} floor\), a unique shortest path joins \(x\) and \(y\) Unique step closer For \(1 \le i = \delta(x, y) \le n - 1\), \(\lvert \widetilde{\Gamma}_{i-1}(x) \cap \widetilde{\Gamma}_1(y) vert = 1\) For \(1 \le i = d(x, y) \le \lfloor rac{n-1}{2} floor\), \(\lvert \Gamma_{i-1}(x) \cap \Gamma_1(y) vert = 1\) Non-backtracking walks Walk \(x_0, \dots, x_k\) with \(k \le n\) and \(x_{r-1} eq x_{r+1}\) has \(\delta(x_0, x_k) = k\) Walk \(x_0, \dots, x_k\) with \(k \le \lfloor rac{n}{2} floor\) and \(x_{r-1}x_r eq x_r x_{r+1}\) has \(d(x_0, x_k) = k\) Diameter \(\operatorname{diam}(\widetilde{\Gamma}) = n\) \(\operatorname{diam}(\Gamma) = \lfloor rac{n}{2} floor\)

docs.title: Opposite elements, flag apartments, doubling, and orders
docs.text:
The geodesic rules above unlock five further properties of generalized polygons, illustrated in Figure 17(b).

Opposite vertices in \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) have equal degree. Start with a general observation about any bipartite graph (not necessarily complete) \(G\) of diameter \(n \ge 2\) in which \(\lvert G_{n-2}(u) \cap G_1(v) \rvert = 1\) whenever \(d_G(u, v) = n - 1\). Here, \(G_k(u)\) is the set of vertices at distance \(k\) from \(u\). Essentially, if two vertices \(u\) and \(v\) are at distance \(n - 1\), then standing at \(v\), there is one and only one edge out of \(v\) that steps closer to \(u\) (to distance \(n - 2\)).

To see why, take any two vertices \(x\) and \(y\) of \(G\) at maximal distance \(d_G(x, y) = n\), as in the top box of Figure 17(b). Every neighbour \(z \in G_1(x)\) lies at distance \(n - 1\) from \(y\): its distance from \(y\) cannot exceed the diameter \(n\), and it cannot equal \(n\) because \(G\) is bipartite. Therefore \(y\) has a unique neighbour \(\pi_1(z) \in G_1(y)\) at distance \(n - 2\) from \(z\). By the same reasoning, each neighbour \(w \in G_1(y)\) lies at distance \(n - 1\) from \(x\) and determines a unique neighbour \(\pi_2(w) \in G_1(x)\) at distance \(n - 2\) from \(w\). Because \(d_G(z, \pi_1(z)) = n - 2\), \(z\) itself is the unique neighbour of \(x\) at distance \(n - 2\) from \(\pi_1(z)\), so \(\pi_2(\pi_1(z)) = z\) for every \(z \in G_1(x)\), and likewise \(\pi_1(\pi_2(w)) = w\) for every \(w \in G_1(y)\). The maps \(\pi_1 : G_1(x) \to G_1(y)\) and \(\pi_2 : G_1(y) \to G_1(x)\) are inverse bijections, giving \(\lvert G_1(x) \rvert = \lvert G_1(y) \rvert\). Since \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) satisfies \(\lvert \widetilde{\Gamma}_{n-2}(u) \cap \widetilde{\Gamma}_1(v) \rvert = 1\) at distance \(n - 1\), any two vertices of \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) at maximal distance \(n\) from each other have the same degree.

Every two flags lie in a common \(2n\)-cycle. Axiom (GP3') states that any two vertices of \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) lie in a \(2n\)-cycle. In fact, any two flags \(\{p_1, L_1\}\) and \(\{p_2, L_2\}\) of \(\mathcal{S}\) also lie together in a \(2n\)-cycle of \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) (an ordinary \(n\)-gon subgeometry containing \(p_1, L_1, p_2, L_2\)).

To see why, choose \(x_1 \in \{p_1, L_1\}\) and \(x_2 \in \{p_2, L_2\}\) so that \(\delta(x_1, x_2)\) is as large as possible, and let \(y_1, y_2\) be the other elements of the two flags. Because \(x_1, x_2\) maximize the distance and \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) is bipartite, stepping from \(x_2\) to \(y_2\) or from \(x_1\) to \(y_1\) decreases the distance by \(1\):

\[\delta(x_1, y_2) = \delta(x_2, y_1) = \delta(x_1, x_2) - 1.\]

If \(\delta(x_1, x_2) < n\), then the unique shortest path in \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) between \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) must begin with \(x_1, y_1\) and end with \(y_2, x_2\), so it contains all four elements \(p_1, L_1, p_2, L_2\); placing \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) inside a \(2n\)-cycle via (GP3') must use that unique shortest path between them, so the \(2n\)-cycle contains both flags. Suppose instead that \(\delta(x_1, x_2) = n\). Because \(\delta(x_2, y_1) = n - 1\), there is a unique shortest path \(\gamma_1\) of length \(n\) between \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) passing through \(y_1\), and because \(\delta(x_1, y_2) = n - 1\), there is a unique shortest path \(\gamma_2\) of length \(n\) between \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) passing through \(y_2\). If \(\gamma_1 = \gamma_2\), then \(\gamma_1\) contains \(p_1, L_1, p_2, L_2\), and placing \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) in a \(2n\)-cycle via (GP3') completes \(\gamma_1\) to a \(2n\)-cycle: the two halves of that \(2n\)-cycle between \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) are paths of length \(n\), at least one of them differs from \(\gamma_1\), and because any two distinct paths of length \(n\) between opposite vertices meet only at their endpoints (otherwise a shorter part would violate uniqueness of geodesics below \(n\)), that half and \(\gamma_1\) form a \(2n\)-cycle containing \(p_1, L_1, p_2, L_2\). If instead \(\gamma_1 \neq \gamma_2\), then by the same uniqueness of geodesics below \(n\), \(\gamma_1\) and \(\gamma_2\) meet only at their endpoints \(x_1, x_2\), so \(\gamma_1\) and \(\gamma_2\) together form a \(2n\)-cycle containing \(p_1, L_1, p_2, L_2\).

Doubling a generalized \(n\)-gon. Recall that the double \(\mathcal{S}'\) of \(\mathcal{S} = (\mathcal{P}, \mathcal{L}, I)\) takes \(\mathcal{P} \cup \mathcal{L}\) as its point set and the flags \(\{x, L\}\) of \(\mathcal{S}\) as its thin \(2\)-point lines, and that doubling a generalized \(n\)-gon produces a generalized \(2n\)-gon. Our flag-cycle theorem proves this immediately: the incidence graph \(\widetilde{\Gamma}'\) of \(\mathcal{S}'\) is obtained from \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) by inserting each flag \(\{x, L\}\) as a new vertex in the middle of the edge between \(x\) and \(L\) (as shown by the orange diamond on the Heawood graph in Figure 17(a)). Every cycle of \(\widetilde{\Gamma}'\) comes from subdividing a cycle of \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\), doubling the girth from \(2n\) to \(4n\), and because any two vertices or flags of \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) lie in a common \(2n\)-cycle, any two vertices of \(\widetilde{\Gamma}'\) lie in a common \(4n\)-cycle.

Thick generalized \(n\)-gons have an order \((s, t)\), with \(s = t\) when \(n\) is odd. Recall that a partial linear space has order \((s, t)\) when every line has \(s + 1\) points and every point lies on \(t + 1\) lines. Suppose \(\mathcal{S}\) is a thick generalized \(n\)-gon (\(n \ge 3\)), meaning every line is incident with at least \(3\) points and every point is incident with at least \(3\) lines. Then \(\mathcal{S}\) has an order \((s, t)\), and if \(n\) is odd, \(s = t\).

Look at the bottom box of Figure 17(b) to see how thickness forces every point to have the same degree and every line to have the same degree. Every vertex of \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) has degree at least \(3\). Because \(\mathcal{S}\) and \(\mathcal{S}^D\) are connected, showing that all points have the same degree and all lines have the same degree reduces to showing that any two vertices \(x\) and \(y\) of \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) at distance \(\delta(x, y) = 2\) have the same degree. Let \(u\) be the unique common neighbour of \(x\) and \(y\) in \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\). Because \(\deg(u) \ge 3\), we can choose a third neighbour \(z\) of \(u\) distinct from \(x\) and \(y\), and without having to backtrack, we can extend the edge \(uz\) to a path of length \(n - 1\) in \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) ending at some vertex \(v\), which means \(\delta(x, v) = \delta(y, v) = n\). We can be sure that such a path exists and that for example, \(z\) will not "short-circuit" us back to \(x\) or \(y\) too early because in a generalized \(n\)-gon, no short cycles of \(\lt 2n\) are allowed. Thus we can be sure that there is some \(v\) which is at a distance \(n\) from both \(x\) and \(y\). And since opposite vertices at distance \(n\) in \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) have equal degree, \(\deg(x) = \deg(v) = \deg(y)\). Thus \(\mathcal{S}\) has an order \((s, t)\). Moreover, when \(n\) is odd, any two vertices \(x\) and \(y\) at maximal distance \(\delta(x, y) = n\) lie in opposite parts of the bipartite graph \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\), so one is a point (degree \(t + 1\)) and the other is a line (degree \(s + 1\)), and \(\deg(x) = \deg(y)\) gives \(t + 1 = s + 1\), or \(s = t\).

Essentially, it comes down to the fact that every two vertices at distance \(2\) in the incidence graph of a thick generalized \(n\)-gon share an opposite vertex. And since opposite vertices have the same degree, every "alternate" vertex has the same degree. If \(n\) is odd, then lines and points form opposite vertices, so \(s=t\).

Halving thin-lined even generalized polygons. Conversely to doubling, let \(\mathcal{S}\) be a generalized \(2d\)-gon with \(d \ge 3\) in which every line is incident with \(2\) points. Then \(\mathcal{S}\) is isomorphic to the double of a generalized \(d\)-gon.

To prove this, view \(\mathcal{S}\) as a graph \(\Gamma\) whose edges are its \(2\)-point lines. Because \(\mathcal{S}\) is a near \(2d\)-gon, every edge \(\{x_i, x_{i+1}\}\) contains a unique point nearest to any chosen base vertex \(x_0\), so \(d(x_0, x_i)\) and \(d(x_0, x_{i+1})\) have opposite parity. Along any path or cycle \(x_0, x_1, \dots, x_k\) in \(\Gamma\), the distance \(d(x_0, x_i)\) changes parity at every step, so \(d(x_0, x_k)\) and \(k\) have the same parity. For a closed cycle (\(x_k = x_0\), distance \(0\)), the length \(k\) must therefore be even, which means \(\Gamma\) is bipartite. Because the incidence graph \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) of \(\mathcal{S}\) is obtained by subdividing each edge of \(\Gamma\) once and satisfies (GP1')–(GP3') with \(n = 2d\), the bipartite graph \(\Gamma\) itself satisfies (GP1')–(GP3') with \(n = d\). Thus \(\Gamma\) is the incidence graph of a generalized \(d\)-gon \(\mathcal{S}'\). The double \(\mathcal{S}''\) of \(\mathcal{S}'\) is a generalized \(2d\)-gon whose collinearity graph is \(\Gamma\), and because \(2d \ge 6 \ge 4\), our clique-reconstruction theorem gives \(\mathcal{S} \cong \mathcal{S}''\).

docs.title: Three characterizations of generalized polygons
docs.text: Checking (GP3) directly requires finding an ordinary \(n\)-gon subgeometry for every pair of elements. Three characterizations replace (GP3) by simpler global or local conditions.

docs.title: Characterization by diameter and girth of the incidence graph
docs.text:
Recall that any graph of finite girth \(g\) has diameter at least \(\lfloor g / 2 \rfloor\), so a bipartite graph of girth \(2n\) always has diameter at least \(n\). Generalized \(n\)-gons are the geometries that hit that minimum diameter.

Diameter-and-girth characterization. Let \(n \ge 2\) and let \(\mathcal{S} = (\mathcal{P}, \mathcal{L}, I)\) be a point-line geometry. Then \(\mathcal{S}\) is a generalized \(n\)-gon if and only if its incidence graph \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) has diameter \(n\) and girth \(2n\). To see why the incidence graph \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) of a generalized \(n\)-gon has diameter at most \(n\), let us say the diameter of \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) is greater than \(n\). Then there are two vertices \(x\) and \(y\) of \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) with distance \(\delta(x, y) \gt n\). On any cycle of length \(2n\), however, we can go between any two vertices around the shorter way in at most \(n\) steps, so any two vertices on a \(2n\)-cycle are at distance at most \(n\) from each other. Because \(\delta(x, y) \gt n\), the vertices \(x\) and \(y\) cannot lie on a common \(2n\)-cycle, and since a \(2n\)-cycle in \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) is an ordinary \(n\)-gon subgeometry, this contradicts the requirement (GP3) (or its graph form (GP3')) that any two vertices of \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) must sit on an ordinary \(n\)-gon subgeometry.

docs.title: Characterization via near 2n-gons
docs.text:
Every generalized \(2n\)-gon (\(n \ge 2\)) is a near \(2n\)-gon satisfying \(\lvert \Gamma_{i-1}(x) \cap \Gamma_1(y) vert = 1\) whenever \(1 \le i = d(x, y) \le n - 1\). Conversely, a near \(2n\)-gon with that unique-step-closer property is a generalized \(2n\)-gon as soon as it avoids having points of degree \(1\).

Near \(2n\)-gon characterization. Let \(\mathcal{S}\) be a near \(2n\)-gon (\(n \ge 2\)) such that \(\lvert \Gamma_{i-1}(x) \cap \Gamma_1(y) vert = 1\) for every \(i \in \{1, 2, \dots, n - 1\}\) and every two points \(x, y\) with \(d(x, y) = i\). Then five conditions are equivalent:

  1. \(\mathcal{S}\) is a generalized \(2n\)-gon;
  2. for every point \(x\) of \(\mathcal{S}\), there is a point \(y\) at distance \(n\) from \(x\);
  3. \(\lvert \Gamma_{n-1}(x) \cap \Gamma_1(y) vert \ge 2\) for every two points \(x\) and \(y\) at distance \(n\) from each other;
  4. there exist two points \(x\) and \(y\) at distance \(n\) from each other with \(\lvert \Gamma_{n-1}(x) \cap \Gamma_1(y) vert \ge 2\);
  5. every point \(x\) is incident with at least two lines.

Let us trace why all five conditions are equivalent. First check that the incidence graph \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) of \(\mathcal{S}\) has diameter \(2n\). Because \(\mathcal{S}\) has diameter \(n\), the largest distance in \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) between two points is \(2n\). For any point \(x\) and line \(L\), the near-polygon axiom gives a unique point on \(L\) nearest to \(x\), which forces \(d(x, L) \le n - 1\) and \(\delta(x, L) = 2\,d(x, L) + 1 \le 2n - 1\). And for any two lines \(L_1, L_2\), picking a point \(x_1 \in L_1\) gives \(\delta(x_1, L_2) \le 2n - 1\) and hence \(\delta(L_1, L_2) \le 2n\).

Second, check that \(\lvert \widetilde{\Gamma}_{j-1}(u) \cap \widetilde{\Gamma}_1(v) vert = 1\) for every pair of vertices \(u, v\) of \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) at distance \(j \in \{1, 2, \dots, 2n - 1\}\), across all four combinations of points and lines. If \(u = x\) and \(v = y\) are two points at distance \(\delta(x, y) = 2i\) (\(1 \le i \le n - 1\)), a line through \(y\) at distance \(2i - 1\) from \(x\) in \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) must contain a point at distance \(i - 1\) from \(x\), which singles out the unique line \(yz\) through the lone point \(z \in \Gamma_{i-1}(x) \cap \Gamma_1(y)\). If \(u = x\) is a point and \(v = L\) is a line at distance \(\delta(x, L) = 2i + 1\) where \(i = d(x, L)\), a neighbour of \(L\) in \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) at distance \(2i\) from \(x\) is a point of \(L\) at distance \(i\) from \(x\), which is unique because \(\mathcal{S}\) is a near polygon. If \(u = L\) is a line and \(v = x\) is a point at distance \(\delta(L, x) = 2i + 1\) where \(i = d(x, L)\), then for \(i = 0\) (\(x \in L\)) the line \(L\) itself is the unique neighbour of \(x\) at distance \(0\) from \(L\); for \(1 \le i \le n - 1\), let \(y\) be the unique point of \(L\) at distance \(i\) from \(x\) and let \(z\) be the unique point collinear with \(x\) at distance \(i - 1\) from \(y\), so any line \(M\) through \(x\) containing a point \(z'\) at distance \(i - 1\) from some point \(y' \in L\) has \(d(x, y') \le 1 + (i - 1) = i\), forcing \(y' = y\), \(z' = z\), and \(M = xz\). Finally, if \(u = L_2\) and \(v = L_1\) are two distinct lines at distance \(\delta(L_1, L_2) = 2i + 2 < 2n\) (so \(i = d(L_1, L_2) \le n - 2\)), we need a unique point \(x_1 \in L_1\) at distance \(i\) from \(L_2\). This is clear when \(i = 0\); if \(i > 0\) and \(L_1\) contained two distinct points \(x_1 eq x_1'\) at distance \(i\) from \(L_2\), let \(x_2, x_2' \in L_2\) be the unique points of \(L_2\) at distance \(i\) from \(x_1, x_1'\). We cannot have \(x_2 = x_2'\) (or \(L_1\) would have two points at distance \(i\) from \(x_2\)), so \(d(x_1, x_2') = i + 1 < n\). Letting \(x_2''\) be the unique point collinear with \(x_2'\) at distance \(i - 1\) from \(x_1'\) gives \(i \le d(x_1, x_2'') \le 1 + (i - 1) = i\), so \(x_2'\) would have two distinct neighbours \(x_2 eq x_2''\) at distance \(i\) from \(x_1\), a contradiction.

Because \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) is bipartite and \(\lvert \widetilde{\Gamma}_{j-1}(u) \cap \widetilde{\Gamma}_1(v) vert = 1\) for all \(1 \le j \le 2n - 1\), \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) contains no cycles shorter than \(4n\). If (1) holds, placing \(x\) (or \(x\) and \(y\)) inside an ordinary \(2n\)-gon subgeometry immediately gives (2), (3), (4), and (5). Conversely, suppose any one of (2), (3), (4), or (5) holds. Each one produces two points \(u, v \in \mathcal{P}\) at maximal distance \(d(u, v) = n\) (\(\delta(u, v) = 2n\)) such that \(v\) lies on at least two lines, and since \(\mathcal{S}\) is a near \(2n\)-gon, every line through \(v\) contains a point at distance \(n - 1\) from \(u\), giving \(\lvert \widetilde{\Gamma}_{2n-1}(u) \cap \widetilde{\Gamma}_1(v) vert \ge 2\) (under (2), pick any point \(v\) on at least two lines and take \(u\) at distance \(n\) from \(v\); under (3) or (4), distinct points in \(\Gamma_{n-1}(u) \cap \Gamma_1(v)\) must lie on distinct lines through \(v\); under (5), take any two points \(u, v\) at distance \(n\)). Choosing two distinct lines \(w_1 eq w_2\) in \(\widetilde{\Gamma}_{2n-1}(u) \cap \widetilde{\Gamma}_1(v)\) and taking the unique shortest paths \(\gamma_1, \gamma_2\) of length \(2n\) between \(u\) and \(v\) through \(w_1\) and \(w_2\) produces a \(4n\)-cycle in \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\). Thus \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) has diameter \(2n\) and girth \(4n\), so \(\mathcal{S}\) is a generalized \(2n\)-gon by the diameter-and-girth characterization.

docs.title: Characterization via generalized Moore geometries
docs.text:
Our third characterization generalizes the layer-counting bound we used on the Petersen graph. In any regular graph of valency \(k\) and diameter \(d\), counting the vertices at each distance from a fixed vertex \(x\) gives \(1\) vertex at distance \(0\), exactly \(k\) at distance \(1\) (at most \(k\) if multiple edges were allowed), at most \(k(k - 1)\) at distance \(2\), and in general at most \(k(k - 1)^{i-1}\) at distance \(i\), so the graph has at most \(1 + k + k(k - 1) + \dots + k(k - 1)^{d-1}\) vertices; this upper bound is the Moore bound, and a graph of valency \(k\) and diameter \(d\) that attains it is called a Moore graph.

To extend this idea to point-line geometries, let \(d, s, t, c\) be positive integers with \(d \ge 2\) (and \(c \le t + 1\)). A generalized Moore geometry of type \(\mathrm{GM}_d(s, t, c)\) is a partial linear space \(\mathcal{S}\) of diameter \(d\) and order \((s, t)\) satisfying two distance-stepping rules for every base point \(x\). First, if \(y\) is a point at distance \(i \in \{1, 2, \dots, d - 1\}\) from \(x\), there is a unique line through \(y\) containing \(1\) point at distance \(i - 1\) from \(x\) and \(s\) points at distance \(i\) from \(x\), while each of the other \(t\) lines through \(y\) contains (besides \(y\)) \(s\) points at distance \(i + 1\) from \(x\). Second, if \(y\) is a point at maximal distance \(d\) from \(x\), there are \(c\) lines through \(y\) containing a (necessarily unique) point at distance \(d - 1\) from \(x\) (and \(s\) points at distance \(d\) from \(x\)), while each of the remaining \(t + 1 - c\) lines through \(y\) has all \(s + 1\) of its points at distance \(d\) from \(x\).

When \(c = 1\), a \(\mathrm{GM}_d(s, t, 1)\) is called a Moore geometry, and when \(s = c = 1\) a \(\mathrm{GM}_d(1, t, 1)\) is a Moore graph of valency \(k = t + 1\) and diameter \(d\) (for example, odd cycles of length \(2d + 1 \ge 5\) and the Petersen graph \(\mathrm{GM}_2(1, 2, 1)\)). At the opposite extreme \(c = t + 1\), every line through \(y \in \Gamma_d(x)\) steps down to distance \(d - 1\) from \(x\).

Generalized Moore geometry characterization. Let \(s, t, d\) be positive integers with \(d \ge 2\). Then the generalized Moore geometries of type \(\mathrm{GM}_d(s, t, t + 1)\) are the generalized \(2d\)-gons of order \((s, t)\).

In one direction, if \(\mathcal{S}\) is a generalized \(2d\)-gon of order \((s, t)\), then \(\mathcal{S}\) has diameter \(d\), the unique-step-closer rule gives the first condition at distance \(i \in \{1, \dots, d - 1\}\), and because \(\mathcal{S}\) is a near \(2d\)-gon, every one of the \(t + 1\) lines through a point \(y\) at distance \(d\) from \(x\) contains a unique point at distance \(d - 1\) from \(x\) (so \(c = t + 1\)). Conversely, suppose \(\mathcal{S}\) is a generalized Moore geometry of type \(\mathrm{GM}_d(s, t, t + 1)\). Because \(c = t + 1\), no line can consist entirely of points at distance \(d\) from \(x\), so every point-line pair \((x, L)\) has \(d(x, L) \le d - 1\), and the first condition guarantees a unique point on \(L\) nearest to \(x\). Thus \(\mathcal{S}\) is a near \(2d\)-gon with \(\lvert \Gamma_{i-1}(x) \cap \Gamma_1(y) \rvert = 1\) for \(1 \le i \le d - 1\) in which every point lies on \(t + 1 \ge 2\) lines, so \(\mathcal{S}\) is a generalized \(2d\)-gon of order \((s, t)\) by the near \(2n\)-gon characterization.

Compare \(c = t + 1\) with \(c = 1\) on the Petersen graph \(\mathrm{GM}_2(1, 2, 1)\) (\(d = 2, s = 1, t = 2, c = 1\)). It is a near \(5\)-gon of diameter \(2\) and girth \(5\), yet it is not a generalized \(5\)-gon: because \(c = 1 < 3 = t + 1\), each vertex \(y\) at distance \(2\) from \(x\) has \(t + 1 - c = 2\) edges lying entirely inside \(\Gamma_2(x)\), so two disjoint edges \(L_1, L_2\) at distance \(d(L_1, L_2) = 2\) sit at distance \(\delta(L_1, L_2) = 2(2) + 2 = 6 > 5\) in the incidence graph \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) (which has girth \(10\) and diameter \(6\) instead of \(5\)).

docs.title: Grids, dual grids, and the order trichotomy
docs.text:
We now zoom in on generalized polygons of diameter \(2\), the generalized quadrangles. When introducing generalized quadrangles earlier, we stated how they split into grids, dual grids, and quadrangles of order \((s, t)\). Let us now prove those classification theorems.

Characterization of grids and dual grids among generalized quadrangles. Let \(\mathcal{S}\) be a generalized quadrangle. If every point of \(\mathcal{S}\) is incident with \(2\) lines, then \(\mathcal{S}\) is a grid. Dually, if every line of \(\mathcal{S}\) is incident with \(2\) points, then \(\mathcal{S}\) is a dual grid.

By point-line duality it suffices to prove the second statement. Suppose every line of the generalized quadrangle \(\mathcal{S}\) has \(2\) points, so \(\mathcal{S}\) can be viewed as a triangle-free graph \(\Gamma\) of diameter \(2\). Fix a point \(x\) of \(\mathcal{S}\). Because \(\Gamma\) has no triangles, no two points of \(\Gamma_1(x)\) are adjacent. Now pick any \(y \in \Gamma_1(x)\) and any \(z \in \Gamma_2(x)\). Since \(z\) does not lie on the \(2\)-point line \(xy\), (GQ2) says that \(z\) is collinear with a unique point of \(xy\); because \(z \in \Gamma_2(x)\) is not collinear with \(x\), that unique point must be \(y\), so \(z \sim y\). Thus every point of \(\{x\} \cup \Gamma_2(x)\) is collinear with every point of \(\Gamma_1(x)\). Because \(\Gamma\) has no triangles and \(\Gamma_1(x)\) is nonempty, no two points of \(\Gamma_2(x)\) can be collinear either. Therefore \(\Gamma\) is a complete bipartite graph with parts \(\{x\} \cup \Gamma_2(x)\) and \(\Gamma_1(x)\), which is a dual grid.

The order trichotomy for generalized quadrangles. For any (finite or infinite) generalized quadrangle \(\mathcal{S}\), one and only one of three cases holds: \(\mathcal{S}\) is a nonsymmetrical grid; \(\mathcal{S}\) is a nonsymmetrical dual grid; or \(\mathcal{S}\) has an order \((s, t)\) (which covers symmetrical grids of order \((s, 1)\), symmetrical dual grids of order \((1, t)\), and all thick generalized quadrangles).

To prove this, suppose \(\mathcal{S}\) is neither a grid nor a dual grid; we must show that \(\mathcal{S}\) has an order \((s, t)\). For each point \(x\) of \(\mathcal{S}\), write \(t_x + 1 \ge 2\) for the number of lines through \(x\). Whenever two points \(x\) and \(y\) are noncollinear, (GQ2) pairs each line through \(x\) with the unique line through \(y\) that meets it, giving a bijection between the lines through \(x\) and the lines through \(y\), so \(t_x = t_y\). Because \(\mathcal{S}\) is not a dual grid, our previous result guarantees at least one line \(L\) with \(3\) or more points. Take any two distinct points \(x, y \in L\), pick a third point \(u \in L\) distinct from \(x\) and \(y\), pick a line \(L_u \neq L\) through \(u\), and pick a point \(z \in L_u \setminus \{u\}\). Because \(\mathcal{S}\) has no triangles, \(z\) is noncollinear with both \(x\) and \(y\), so \(t_x = t_z = t_y\). Hence every point on \(L\) lies on the same number of lines \(t + 1\). And if \(w\) is any point outside \(L\), then \(w\) is collinear with only one point of \(L\) and noncollinear with all remaining points of \(L\), which forces \(t_w = t\) as well. Since \(\mathcal{S}\) is not a grid, some point lies on at least \(3\) lines, and repeating the exact same argument in the dual \(\mathcal{S}^D\) shows that every line of \(\mathcal{S}\) is incident with the same number of points \(s + 1\).

When \(\mathcal{S} = (\mathcal{P}, \mathcal{L}, I)\) is a finite generalized quadrangle of order \((s, t)\) and \(L\) is any line of \(\mathcal{S}\), every point outside \(L\) lies in \(\Gamma_1(L)\) and is collinear with a unique point of \(L\). At each of the \(s + 1\) points of \(L\), there are \(t\) lines other than \(L\), each holding \(s\) points outside \(L\), giving

\[\lvert \mathcal{P} \rvert = \lvert L \rvert + \lvert \Gamma_1(L) \rvert = (s + 1) + (s + 1)st = (s + 1)(st + 1)\]

and, by duality, \(\lvert \mathcal{L} \rvert = (t + 1)(st + 1)\).

docs.title: Classical generalized quadrangles and their dualities
docs.text:
Recall from the projective geometry notes that every polar space of rank \(2\) (Witt index \(2\), whose maximal singular or totally isotropic subspaces are lines) has points and lines forming a generalized quadrangle. Over a commutative field \(\mathbb{F}\) (or a quadratic extension \(\mathbb{F}' / \mathbb{F}\)), these classical families are the nonsingular quadrics \(Q^+(3, \mathbb{F})\) in \(\mathrm{PG}(3, \mathbb{F})\), \(Q(4, \mathbb{F})\) in \(\mathrm{PG}(4, \mathbb{F})\), and \(Q^-(5, \mathbb{F}'/\mathbb{F})\) in \(\mathrm{PG}(5, \mathbb{F})\), the nonsingular \(\sigma\)-Hermitian varieties \(H(3, \mathbb{F}'/\mathbb{F})\) in \(\mathrm{PG}(3, \mathbb{F}')\) and \(H(4, \mathbb{F}'/\mathbb{F})\) in \(\mathrm{PG}(4, \mathbb{F}')\) for a separable quadratic extension \(\mathbb{F}'/\mathbb{F}\) with involutory automorphism \(\sigma\), and the symplectic generalized quadrangle \(W(\mathbb{F}) = W(3, \mathbb{F})\) of all points and totally isotropic lines of a symplectic polarity in \(\mathrm{PG}(3, \mathbb{F})\). Over a finite field \(\mathbb{F}_q\) (with \(\mathbb{F}' = \mathbb{F}_{q^2}\) in the Hermitian cases), their orders and point-line dualities are summarized below:

Classical finite GQ Ambient space Order \((s, t)\) Point count \((s+1)(st+1)\) Duality and isomorphism relations \(Q^+(3, q)\) \(\mathrm{PG}(3, q)\) \((q, 1)\) \((q + 1)^2\) Symmetrical \((q + 1) \times (q + 1)\) grid \(W(q) = W(3, q)\) \(\mathrm{PG}(3, q)\) \((q, q)\) \((q + 1)(q^2 + 1)\) \(W(q) \cong Q(4, q)^D\); and \(W(q) \cong Q(4, q)\) if and only if \(q\) is even \(Q(4, q)\) \(\mathrm{PG}(4, q)\) \((q, q)\) \((q + 1)(q^2 + 1)\) \(Q(4, q) \cong W(q)^D\); self-dual if and only if \(q\) is even \(Q^-(5, q)\) \(\mathrm{PG}(5, q)\) \((q, q^2)\) \((q + 1)(q^3 + 1)\) \(Q^-(5, q)^D \cong H(3, q^2)\) (attains \(t = s^2\)) \(H(3, q^2)\) \(\mathrm{PG}(3, q^2)\) \((q^2, q)\) \((q^2 + 1)(q^3 + 1)\) \(H(3, q^2) \cong Q^-(5, q)^D\) (attains \(s = t^2\)) \(H(4, q^2)\) \(\mathrm{PG}(4, q^2)\) \((q^2, q^3)\) \((q^2 + 1)(q^5 + 1)\) Dual \(H(4, q^2)^D\) has order \((q^3, q^2)\)

docs.title: Triads, centers, and the combinatorial proof of Higman's bound
docs.text:
Earlier we proved Higman's inequality \(t \le s^2\) (for \(s \ge 2\)) from the Krein condition \(q_{22}^2 \ge 0\) on the collinearity graph. A combinatorial counting proof due to Bose and Shrikhande (with the inequality observed by Cameron) reveals what happens inside the generalized quadrangle when \(t\) hits the ceiling \(s^2\), as illustrated in Figure 18(a).

In a generalized quadrangle \(\mathcal{S}\), a triad is a set \(T = \{x, y, z\}\) of three mutually noncollinear points, and any point \(u\) collinear with all three (\(u \in x^\perp \cap y^\perp \cap z^\perp\)) is called a center of \(T\).

Figure 18. Triads, centers, and hyperplane complements in generalized quadrangles. (a) For a fixed noncollinear pair \(\{x, y\}\) in a finite GQ of order \((s, t)\), the \(t + 1\) points of \(x^\perp \cap y^\perp\) send lines into \(Z = \mathcal{P} \setminus (x^\perp \cup y^\perp)\), where each \(z \in Z\) completes \(\{x, y\}\) to a triad with \(t_z = \lvert x^\perp \cap y^\perp \cap z^\perp vert\) centers; nonnegativity of the variance \(\sum_{z \in Z}(t_z - ar{t})^2\) gives \(t \le s^2\), with equality if and only if \(t_z = s + 1\) is constant. (b) For any hyperplane \(H\) of a thick GQ \(\mathcal{S}\), two points \(y_1, y_2 \in \overline{H} = \mathcal{P} \setminus H\) whose common neighbours all lie in \(H\) are joined inside \(\overline{H}\) by a \(3\)-step path \(y_1 \sim y'_1 \sim y'_2 \sim y_2\), so \(\overline{H}\) has diameter at most \(3\).

Combinatorial Higman inequality and triad characterization of \(t = s^2\). Let \(\mathcal{S} = (\mathcal{P}, \mathcal{L}, I)\) be a finite generalized quadrangle of order \((s, t)\) with \(s, t \ge 2\), and let \(x, y\) be two arbitrary noncollinear points of \(\mathcal{S}\). Then \(t \le s^2\), and five conditions are equivalent:

  • \(t = s^2\);
  • every triad of \(\mathcal{S}\) has \(s + 1\) centers;
  • all triads of \(\mathcal{S}\) have a constant number of centers;
  • all triads of \(\mathcal{S}\) containing \(x\) have a constant number of centers;
  • all triads of \(\mathcal{S}\) containing \(x\) and \(y\) have a constant number of centers.

To prove all of this at once, it is enough to show that \(t \le s^2\), with equality if and only if the triads containing the fixed noncollinear pair \(\{x, y\}\) have a constant number of centers, and that this constant is then \(s + 1\). Let \(Z = \mathcal{P} \setminus (x^\perp \cup y^\perp)\) be the set of points noncollinear with both \(x\) and \(y\) (the points \(z\) that complete \(\{x, y\}\) to a triad). Because \(\lvert \mathcal{P} vert = (s + 1)(st + 1)\), \(\lvert \{x, y\} vert = 2\), \(\lvert x^\perp \setminus \{x\} vert = \lvert y^\perp \setminus \{y\} vert = (t + 1)s\), and \(\lvert x^\perp \cap y^\perp vert = t + 1\) (with \(x otin y^\perp\) and \(y otin x^\perp\)), inclusion-exclusion gives

\[\lvert Z vert = (s + 1)(st + 1) - 2 - 2(t + 1)s + (t + 1) = s^2 t - st - s + t > 0.\]

For each \(z \in Z\), write \(t_z = \lvert x^\perp \cap y^\perp \cap z^\perp vert\) for the number of centers of \(\{x, y, z\}\). First count in two ways the pairs \((z, u)\) where \(z \in Z\) and \(u \in x^\perp \cap y^\perp \cap z^\perp\). There are \(t + 1\) choices for \(u \in x^\perp \cap y^\perp\). Once \(u\) is chosen, the \(t + 1\) lines through \(u\) consist of \(ux\), \(uy\), and \(t - 1\) other lines; on each of those \(t - 1\) other lines, all \(s\) points other than \(u\) belong to \(Z\) (none can be collinear with \(x\) or \(y\) without creating a triangle). That gives

\[\sum_{z \in Z} t_z = (t + 1)(t - 1)s.\]

Next count in two ways the ordered triples \((z, u, u')\) where \(z \in Z\) and \(u, u' \in x^\perp \cap y^\perp \cap z^\perp\) with \(u eq u'\). There are \(t + 1\) choices for \(u \in x^\perp \cap y^\perp\), and then \(t\) choices for \(u' \in (x^\perp \cap y^\perp) \setminus \{u\}\). Because \(u\) and \(u'\) are distinct common neighbours of \(x\) and \(y\) and \(\mathcal{S}\) has no triangles, \(u\) and \(u'\) are noncollinear. On each of the \(t - 1\) lines through \(u\) distinct from \(ux\) and \(uy\), (GQ2) gives a unique point \(z\) collinear with \(u'\), and that point \(z\) lies in \(Z\). Hence

\[\sum_{z \in Z} t_z(t_z - 1) = (t + 1)t(t - 1),\]

and adding our first sum to this one gives

\[\sum_{z \in Z} t_z^2 = (t + 1)(t - 1)(s + t).\]

Let \( ar{t} = \lvert Z vert^{-1} \sum_{z \in Z} t_z\) be the average of \(t_z\) over \(z \in Z\). The variance sum \(\sum_{z \in Z} (t_z - ar{t})^2 \ge 0\) is equivalent to \(\lvert Z vert \sum_{z \in Z} t_z^2 - igl(\sum_{z \in Z} t_z igr)^2 \ge 0\), which substitutes and factors as

\[(s^2 t - st - s + t)(t^2 - 1)(s + t) - (t^2 - 1)^2 s^2 = t(t^2 - 1)(s - 1)(s^2 - t) \ge 0.\]

Since \(s, t \ge 2\), the factor \(t(t^2 - 1)(s - 1)\) is strictly positive, so \(s^2 - t \ge 0\), or \(t \le s^2\). Equality \(t = s^2\) holds if and only if \(t_z = ar{t}\) for every \(z \in Z\), in which case substituting \(t = s^2\) gives

\[ ar{t} = rac{(s^2 + 1)(s^2 - 1)s}{s^4 - s^3 + s^2 - s} = rac{(s^2 + 1)(s + 1)(s - 1)s}{(s^2 + 1)(s - 1)s} = s + 1.\]

We can see the difference between \(t < s^2\) and \(t = s^2\) on two small classical quadrangles with \(s = 2\). In the \(15\)-point doily \(W(2)\) (Figure 9, with \(s = t = 2 < s^2\)), represent the \(15\) points as the \(2\)-element subsets of \(\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}\), collinear when disjoint, and fix the noncollinear pair \(x = \{1, 2\}\) and \(y = \{1, 3\}\). Their \(t + 1 = 3\) common neighbours are \(\{4, 5\}, \{4, 6\}, \{5, 6\}\), and \(Z\) consists of the \(\lvert Z vert = 4\) subsets \(\{1, 4\}, \{1, 5\}, \{1, 6\}, \{2, 3\}\). Each of \(\{1, 4\}, \{1, 5\}, \{1, 6\}\) is disjoint from only \(1\) of the three common neighbours (\(t_z = 1\) center), whereas \(z = \{2, 3\}\) is disjoint from all \(3\) of them (\(t_z = 3\) centers), matching \(\sum t_z = 6\) and \(\sum t_z^2 = 12\) with positive variance.

In the \(27\)-point elliptic quadric \(Q^-(5, 2)\) (\(s = 2, t = 4 = s^2\)), each point \(x\) has \(\lvert x^\perp vert = 1 + 2(5) = 11\), leaving \(27 - 11 = 16\) choices for a point \(y\) noncollinear with \(x\) and \(\lvert Z vert = 10\) choices for a third point \(z\) noncollinear with both. That gives \(27 imes 16 imes 10 / 6 = 720\) triads in total, and because \(t = s^2\) holds, \(\sum t_z = 30\) and \(\sum t_z^2 = 90\) have variance \(10(90) - 30^2 = 0\): every one of the \(720\) triads has \(s + 1 = 3\) centers.

docs.title: Subquadrangles and hyperplane complements
docs.text:
Recall that in a partial linear space \(\mathcal{S} = (\mathcal{P}, \mathcal{L}, I)\), a subset \(X \subseteq \mathcal{P}\) is a subspace when every line meeting \(X\) in at least two points lies wholly in \(X\), and a hyperplane is a proper subspace that meets every line. In a generalized quadrangle \(\mathcal{S}\), a subgeometry (respectively, a full subgeometry) of \(\mathcal{S}\) that is itself a generalized quadrangle is called a subquadrangle (respectively, a full subquadrangle) of \(\mathcal{S}\).

Subspaces and full subquadrangles. Let \(\mathcal{S} = (\mathcal{P}, \mathcal{L}, I)\) be a generalized quadrangle. If \(X\) is a subspace of \(\mathcal{S}\) containing two disjoint lines \(L_1\) and \(L_2\), then the full subgeometry \(\widetilde{X}\) induced on \(X\) is a full subquadrangle of \(\mathcal{S}\). Conversely, every full subquadrangle of \(\mathcal{S}\) has the form \(\widetilde{Y}\) for some subspace \(Y\) of \(\mathcal{S}\) containing two disjoint lines.

Why are these two aspects connected? Why is it sufficient for a subspace to just have 2 disjoint lines to become a generalized quadrangle in its own right? The two disjoint lines \(L_1, L_2\) are only there to give (GQ1), which asks for two lines that do not meet. The real work is (GQ2), and it has to hold for every point \(x\) of \(X\) and every line \(L\) of \(X\) not through \(x\). Since \(X\) is a subspace, lines are "imported" with all their points from the main quadrangle. In \(\mathcal{S}\), (GQ2) gives a unique point \(y\) on \(L\) collinear with \(x\), and \(y\) is present in the subspace because \(L\) is imported whole. How do we know the connecting line \(xy\) is present in the subspace? It meets \(X\) in the two points \(x\) and \(y\), and since \(X\) is a subspace, the entire line must be in \(X\). So \(y\) is collinear with \(x\) inside the subspace too, and no other point of \(L\) can be, since it would already be collinear with \(x\) in \(\mathcal{S}\). For example, a point \(p_1\) on \(L_1\) keeps its line back to \(L_2\) inside the subspace.

Connectivity and diameter of hyperplane complements. Suppose \(\mathcal{S}\) is a generalized quadrangle that is not a dual grid, and let \(H\) be a hyperplane of \(\mathcal{S}\). Then the subgraph of the collinearity graph \(\Gamma\) induced on the complement \(\overline{H} = \mathcal{P} \setminus H\) is connected and has diameter at most \(3\).

The subgraph of the collinearity graph induced on \(\overline{H}\) means you start with the collinearity graph \(\Gamma\) of the generalized quadrangle \(\mathcal{S}\) and delete every point belonging to the hyperplane \(H\) (along with any graph edges attached to those deleted points), leaving only the points outside \(H\) and the collinearity connections between them.

For a dual grid, \(s = 1\), where lines only have \(2\) points. Deleting a point means only one point of the line in the complement, which means no two points are collinear, which is why we set the condition.

This theorem is saying that in the full quadrangle \(\mathcal{S}\), the collinearity graph \(\Gamma\) has diameter \(2\) (any two noncollinear points \(x, y\) have a common neighbor \(z\), giving a path \(x \sim z \sim y\) of length \(2\)). If you delete \(H\), it might happen that all \(t + 1\) common neighbors of \(x\) and \(y\) were sitting inside \(H\) and got deleted. Even in that worst-case scenario, you never have to take a detour longer than \(3\) steps (\(x \sim w_1 \sim w_2 \sim y\), with \(w_1, w_2 \notin H\)) to get from \(x\) to \(y\).

Now for the proof. Let us check both the thin-line case and the thick-line case (drawn in Figure 18(b)). If \(\mathcal{S}\) has lines of size \(2\), then because \(\mathcal{S}\) is not a dual grid, our order trichotomy says that \(\mathcal{S}\) is a \((2 \times k)\)-grid for some \(k \ge 3\), with two lines \(L_1, L_2\) of size \(k\) and \(k\) thin lines of size \(2\). Every one of the \(k \ge 3\) thin lines meets \(H\), so at least one of \(L_1, L_2\), say \(L_1\), contains at least two points of \(H\) and hence lies wholly in \(H\). Then \(L_2\) meets \(H\) in a unique point \(x'\) (otherwise \(H\) would contain all of \(\mathcal{P}\)), and if \(x\) is the unique point of \(L_1\) collinear with \(x'\), we have \(H = x^\perp\). Its complement \(\overline{H} = L_2 \setminus \{x'\}\) consists of \(k - 1 \ge 2\) collinear points on \(L_2\), so it is connected of diameter \(1\).

Now suppose every line of \(\mathcal{S}\) has at least \(3\) points, and take two distinct points \(y_1, y_2 \in \overline{H}\). If \(d(y_1, y_2) = 1\), then \(y_1\) and \(y_2\) are adjacent in \(\overline{H}\) and have distance \(1\) in \(\overline{H}\). If \(d(y_1, y_2) = 2\) and \(\Gamma_1(y_1) \cap \Gamma_1(y_2) \cap \overline{H} \neq \emptyset\), then a common neighbour in \(\overline{H}\) joins \(y_1\) to \(y_2\) in \(2\) steps inside \(\overline{H}\). Finally, if \(d(y_1, y_2) = 2\) and \(\Gamma_1(y_1) \cap \Gamma_1(y_2) \subseteq H\) (the worst case, shown in Figure 18(b)), pick two distinct common neighbours \(z_1, z_2 \in \Gamma_1(y_1) \cap \Gamma_1(y_2) \subseteq H\). Because the line \(y_2 z_2\) has at least \(3\) points and meets \(H\) only at \(z_2\), we can choose a point \(y'_2\) on \(y_2 z_2\) distinct from \(y_2\) and \(z_2\), so \(y'_2 \in \overline{H}\). Then \(y'_2\) is not collinear with \(z_1\) because \(y_2\) is the unique point of the line \(y_2 z_2\) collinear with \(z_1\), and \(y'_2\) is not collinear with \(y_1\) because \(z_2\) is the unique point of \(y_2 z_2\) collinear with \(y_1\). Therefore, on the line \(y_1 z_1\), the unique point \(y'_1\) collinear with \(y'_2\) is distinct from both \(y_1\) and \(z_1\), which means \(y'_1 \in \overline{H}\) (since \(y_1 z_1\) meets \(H\) only at \(z_1\)). The path \(y_1, y'_1, y'_2, y_2\) lies wholly inside \(\overline{H}\), so \(y_1\) and \(y_2\) have distance \(3\) in \(\overline{H}\).

In any generalized quadrangle \(\mathcal{S}\), the set \(x^\perp\) is a hyperplane for every point \(x\) (each line through \(x\) lies inside \(x^\perp\), and each line missing \(x\) meets \(x^\perp\) in a unique point by (GQ2)). Applying the theorem to \(H = x^\perp\) shows that if \(\mathcal{S}\) is not a dual grid, then \(\Gamma_2(x) = \mathcal{P} \setminus x^\perp\) is connected and has diameter at most \(3\) for every point \(x\) of \(\mathcal{S}\) (whereas in a dual grid \(K_{a, b}\) with \(a \ge 3\), a vertex \(x\) in the part of size \(a\) has \(\Gamma_2(x)\) equal to the other \(a - 1 \ge 2\) vertices in its own part, an independent set with no edges at all).

docs.title: The theorem of Feit and Higman
Distance-regularity of the collinearity graph and point counts
docs.text:
Now let \(\mathcal{S}\) be a finite generalized \(n\)-gon (\(n \ge 3\)) of order \((s, t)\), with collinearity graph \(\Gamma\). Recall that a connected graph of diameter \(d\) is distance-regular when, for every distance \(i \in \{0, 1, \dots, d\}\) and every pair of vertices \(x, y\) at distance \(i\), the numbers \(c_i = \lvert \Gamma_{i-1}(x) \cap \Gamma_1(y) \rvert\), \(a_i = \lvert \Gamma_i(x) \cap \Gamma_1(y) \rvert\), and \(b_i = \lvert \Gamma_{i+1}(x) \cap \Gamma_1(y) \rvert\) depend only on \(i\), and that the sphere sizes \(k_i = \lvert \Gamma_i(x) \rvert\) are then determined by \(k_0 = 1\) and \(k_{i+1} = k_i b_i / c_{i+1}\).

When \(n \ge 4\), our geodesic rules (such as a unique geodesic between two vertices) in \(\Gamma\) make \(\Gamma\) distance-regular of diameter \(d = \lfloor \frac{n}{2} \rfloor\), with parameters read straight off Figure 19(a). At \(i = 0\), \(a_0 = c_0 = 0\) and \(b_0 = s(t + 1)\) (the valency \(k\) of \(\Gamma\): \(t + 1\) lines through \(x\), each holding \(s\) neighbours of \(x\)).

For \(i \in \{1, 2, \dots, d - 1\}\), any point \(y \in \Gamma_i(x)\) lies on a unique line containing a (necessarily unique) point at distance \(i - 1\) from \(x\). Why is there only one such line through \(y\)? If there were two lines through \(y\), each containing a point at distance \(i - 1\) (say \(z_1\) and \(z_2\)), then a shortest path from \(x\) to \(z_1\), the two steps \(z_1 \to y \to z_2\), and a shortest path from \(z_2\) back to \(x\) would close up into a closed walk of length \((i - 1) + 2 + (i - 1) = 2i\) in \(\Gamma\). A short closed walk in \(\Gamma\) is not a contradiction by itself, since the points of a line already form triangles. The contradiction is in the incidence graph \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\), where every step between collinear points becomes two steps (point, line, point). There, the two routes from \(x\) to \(y\) through \(z_1\) and through \(z_2\) are two different paths of length \(2i\) between the same two vertices, and two such paths always contain a cycle of length at most \(2i + 2i = 4i\). Since \(i < \frac{n}{2}\), this is less than \(2n\), contradicting the girth \(2n\) of \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\).

Continuing, on this line containing \(y\) and the unique point, its other \(s - 1\) points lie at distance \(i\) from \(x\). This is because if another point \(z'\) of the line were also at distance \(i - 1\), the shortest paths from \(x\) to \(z\) and to \(z'\) together with the step \(z \to z'\) would give a closed walk of length \(2i - 1\) in \(\Gamma\), and in \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) two different paths of length \(2i - 1\) from \(x\) to the line (one through \(z\), one through \(z'\)), which contain a cycle of length at most \(4i - 2 < 2n\). How do we know none of the points are at a distance \(i+1\)? Because every point on this line is at a distance 1 from \(z\) and therefore must have a distance at most \(i\), not \(i+1\).

Continuing, all \(t\) remaining lines through \(y\) step out to distance \(i + 1\) from \(x\). None of their points can be at distance \(i\): such a point \(w\) on a line \(M\) through \(y\) would give two different paths of length \(2i + 1\) from \(x\) to \(M\) in \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) (one through \(y\), one through \(w\)), and so a cycle of length at most \(4i + 2\), which is less than \(2n\) because \(i \le \lfloor \frac{n}{2} \rfloor - 1\). None of them can be at distance \(i - 1\) either, because then \(M\) would be a second line through \(y\) containing a point at distance \(i - 1\), which we have just ruled out.

This gives \(c_i = 1\), \(a_i = s - 1\), and \(b_i = s(t + 1) - a_i - c_i = st\). At the opposite layer \(i = d\) (where \(b_d = 0\)), if \(n = 2d\) is even, then \(\mathcal{S}\) is a near \(2d\)-gon so each of the \(t + 1\) lines through \(y \in \Gamma_d(x)\) contains \(1\) point at distance \(d - 1\) from \(x\) and \(s - 1\) other points at distance \(d\) from \(x\), giving \(c_d = t + 1\) and \(a_d = (s - 1)(t + 1)\); if \(n = 2d + 1\) is odd, then \(d = \frac{n - 1}{2} = \lfloor \frac{n - 1}{2} \rfloor\), so only \(1\) line through \(y\) contains a unique point at distance \(d - 1\) from \(x\), giving \(c_d = 1\) and \(a_d = st + s - 1\).

Figure 19. Distance-regularity of the collinearity graph \(\Gamma\) and the Feit–Higman classification. (a) For any finite generalized \(n\)-gon (\(n \ge 4\)) of order \((s, t)\), the collinearity graph \(\Gamma\) has diameter \(d = \lfloor n / 2 \rfloor\), step parameters \(b_0 = s(t + 1)\) and \(b_i = st\), \(c_i = 1\), \(a_i = s - 1\) for \(1 \le i < d\), and opposite-layer parameters \(c_d = t + 1, a_d = (s - 1)(t + 1)\) for even \(n\) versus \(c_d = 1, a_d = st + s - 1\) for odd \(n\). (b) Summary of all finite generalized \(n\)-gons (\(n \ge 3\)) having an order \((s, t)\): thick examples occur only for \(n \in \{3, 4, 6, 8\}\), semi-thin orders \((1, q)\) or \((q, 1)\) arise from grids, dual grids, and doubles at \(n \in \{4, 6, 8, 12\}\), and all other \(n \ge 5\) admit only ordinary \(n\)-gons (\(s = t = 1\)).

Multiplying \(k_{i+1} = k_i b_i / c_{i+1}\) step by step from \(k_0 = 1\) gives the sphere sizes \(k_i = \lvert \Gamma_i(x) \rvert\) for every point \(x\):

\[k_0 = 1, \qquad k_i = s^i t^{i-1}(t + 1) \quad (1 \le i \le d - 1),\] \[k_d = \begin{cases} s^d t^{d-1} & \text{if } n \text{ is even } (c_d = t + 1), \\ s^d t^{d-1}(t + 1) & \text{if } n \text{ is odd } (c_d = 1). \end{cases}\]

Notice that the formula for \(k_d\) branches on whether \(n\) is even or odd, because \(c_d = t + 1\) for even \(n = 2d\) cancels the factor \(t + 1\) in \(k_{d-1} b_{d-1} = s^d t^{d-1}(t + 1)\), whereas \(c_d = 1\) for odd \(n = 2d + 1\) keeps it. Summing \(v = k_0 + k_1 + \dots + k_d\) for a finite generalized \(2d\)-gon of order \((s, t)\) (\(d \ge 2\), so \(n = 2d\) is even) factors cleanly:

\[v = 1 + (t + 1)s\bigl(1 + st + \dots + (st)^{d-2}\bigr) + s^d t^{d-1} = (s + 1)\bigl(1 + st + (st)^2 + \dots + (st)^{d-1}\bigr).\]

In particular, a finite generalized quadrangle (\(2d = 4\)) has \(v = (s + 1)(1 + st)\) points, a finite generalized hexagon (\(2d = 6\)) has \(v = (s + 1)(1 + st + s^2 t^2)\) points, and a finite generalized octagon (\(2d = 8\)) has \(v = (s + 1)(1 + st + s^2 t^2 + s^3 t^3)\) points.

docs.title: Rational cosines, the bottom eigenvalue, and the spectral proof
docs.text:
Recall from the Bose–Mesner algebra that for a distance-regular graph \(\Gamma\) of diameter \(d \ge 2\) and valency \(k = b_0\), the normalized polynomials \(u_0(X), u_1(X), \dots, u_d(X)\) are defined by \(u_0(X) = 1\), \(u_1(X) = X / k\), and the recurrence \(b_i u_{i+1}(X) + (a_i - X)u_i(X) + c_i u_{i-1}(X) = 0\) for \(1 \le i \le d - 1\); that the minimal polynomial of \(A\) has degree \(d + 1\) and is proportional to \((X - a_d)u_d(X) - c_d u_{d-1}(X)\) (so \(\Gamma\) has \(d + 1\) distinct eigenvalues); and that for each eigenvalue \( heta\) with standard sequence \( igl(u_0( heta), \dots, u_d( heta) igr)\), Biggs' multiplicity formula gives \(f( heta) = v / \sum_{i=0}^d k_i u_i( heta)^2\).

Two short lemmas prepare the proof of the Feit–Higman theorem.

Rational cosine lemma. For an integer \(n \ge 2\), \(\cos igl( rac{2\pi}{n} igr)\) is rational if and only if \(n \in \{2, 3, 4, 6\}\).

Checking \(n \in \{2, 3, 4, 6\}\) gives \(\cos igl( rac{2\pi}{n} igr) \in \{-1, - rac{1}{2}, 0, rac{1}{2}\}\), all rational. For the converse, here are two ways to see why no other \(n \ge 2\) works. First, let \(\zeta_n = \cos rac{2\pi}{n} + i \sin rac{2\pi}{n}\), which satisfies \(X^2 - 2\cos rac{2\pi}{n}\,X + 1 = 0\). If \(\cos rac{2\pi}{n} \in \mathbb{Q}\), the minimal polynomial of \(\zeta_n\) over \(\mathbb{Q}\) (the \(n\)-th cyclotomic polynomial, of degree \(\varphi(n)\) where \(\varphi\) is Euler's totient function) has degree \(\varphi(n) \in \{1, 2\}\); writing \(\varphi(n) = rac{n}{p_1 \cdots p_k}(p_1 - 1)\cdots(p_k - 1)\) for the distinct prime factors \(p_i\) of \(n\) forces each \(p_i - 1 \le 2\), so \(\{p_1, \dots, p_k\} \subseteq \{2, 3\}\), and checking \(2^{k_1} 3^{k_2}\) leaves only \(n \in \{2, 3, 4, 6\}\). Second, an elementary argument of Coxeter avoids cyclotomic polynomials altogether: suppose \(\cos\phi = rac{a}{b} \in \mathbb{Q}\) in lowest terms with \(b \ge 3\). Then \(\cos(2\phi) = 2\cos^2\phi - 1 = rac{2a^2 - b^2}{b^2}\); when written in lowest terms as \( rac{a'}{b'}\) (\(b' > 0\), \(\gcd(a', b') = 1\)), its denominator is \(b' = b^2 > b\) if \(b\) is odd and \(b' = rac{b^2}{2} > b\) if \(b \ge 4\) is even. Doubling the angle repeatedly (\(\phi, 2\phi, 4\phi, 8\phi, \dots\)) would therefore produce infinitely many distinct rational numbers \(\cos(2^m \phi)\), which is impossible for \(\phi = rac{2\pi}{n}\) because the sequence \(\cos igl(2^m rac{2\pi}{n} igr)\) takes only finitely many values. Thus \(b \in \{1, 2\}\) in lowest terms, giving \(\cos rac{2\pi}{n} \in \{0, \pm 1, \pm rac{1}{2}\}\) and \(n \in \{2, 3, 4, 6\}\).

Bottom eigenvalue of a finite generalized \(2d\)-gon. If \(\mathcal{S}\) is a finite generalized \(2d\)-gon (\(d \ge 2\)) of order \((s, t)\), then \( heta = -t - 1\) is an eigenvalue of \(\Gamma\) with standard sequence \( igl(1, - rac{1}{s}, (- rac{1}{s})^2, \dots, (- rac{1}{s})^d igr)\).

To check this, note that \(u_0( heta) = 1\) and \(u_1( heta) = rac{-t - 1}{s(t + 1)} = - rac{1}{s}\). For every \(i \in \{1, 2, \dots, d - 1\}\), where \(b_i = st\), \(a_i = s - 1\), and \(c_i = 1\), substituting \(u_j( heta) = (- rac{1}{s})^j\) into the three-term recurrence gives

\[st\left(- rac{1}{s} ight)^{i+1} + (s - 1 + t + 1)\left(- rac{1}{s} ight)^i + 1\left(- rac{1}{s} ight)^{i-1} = \left(- rac{1}{s} ight)^{i-1}\left( rac{t}{s} - rac{s + t}{s} + 1 ight) = 0,\]

so \(u_i(-t - 1) = (- rac{1}{s})^i\) for all \(0 \le i \le d\). At the minimal-polynomial boundary \(m(X) = (X - a_d)u_d(X) - c_d u_{d-1}(X)\) (with \(a_d = (s - 1)(t + 1)\) and \(c_d = t + 1\)), evaluating at \( heta = -t - 1\) gives

\[ igl(-t - 1 - (s - 1)(t + 1) igr)\left(- rac{1}{s} ight)^d - (t + 1)\left(- rac{1}{s} ight)^{d-1} = 0,\]

proving that \( heta = -t - 1\) is a root of the minimal polynomial of \(A\) and hence an eigenvalue of \(\Gamma\).

We now have everything needed to prove the Feit–Higman theorem stated earlier: any finite generalized \(n\)-gon \(\mathcal{S}\) (\(n \ge 3\)) of order \((s, t)\) is either an ordinary \(n\)-gon (\(s = t = 1\)), or has \(n \in \{3, 4, 6, 8, 12\}\) with \(s = t \ge 2\) at \(n = 3\), \(st\) a square at \(n = 6\) when \(s eq 1 eq t\), \(2st\) a square at \(n = 8\) when \(s eq 1 eq t\), and \(s = 1\) or \(t = 1\) at \(n = 12\) (so thick finite generalized \(n\)-gons exist only for \(n \in \{2, 3, 4, 6, 8\}\)).

Let us walk through C. Roos's distance-regular proof of the Feit–Higman theorem. First dispose of the small cases. By (GP2), \(\mathcal{S}\) contains an ordinary \(n\)-gon subgeometry \(\mathcal{S}'\); if \(s = t = 1\), then \(\mathcal{S} = \mathcal{S}'\) is an ordinary \(n\)-gon. Assume from now on that at least one of \(s, t\) is greater than \(1\). If \(n = 3\), our small-\(n\) equivalence says \(\mathcal{S}\) is a projective plane of order \((s, t)\) with \((s, t) eq (1, 1)\), so it is a nondegenerate projective plane of order \(s = t \ge 2\). Assume from now on that \(n \ge 4\), so \(\Gamma\) is distance-regular of diameter \(d = \lfloor rac{n}{2} floor\) with \(d + 1\) distinct eigenvalues (and note that if \(n\) is odd, opposite-vertex degree equality between a point and a line at distance \(\delta = n\) in \(\widetilde{\Gamma}\) gives \(s + 1 = t + 1\), so \((s, t) eq (1, 1)\) forces \(s = t > 1\)).

Second, parametrize any eigenvalue \( heta\) of \(\Gamma\) by choosing a nonzero complex number \(\eta \in \mathbb{C} \setminus \{0\}\) such that

\[ heta = \sqrt{st}(\eta + \eta^{-1}) + s - 1.\]

The valency \( heta_0 = k = s(t + 1)\) corresponds to \(\eta \in \{\sqrt{st}, rac{1}{\sqrt{st}}\}\), and when \(n\) is even our bottom-eigenvalue lemma gives \( heta_d = -t - 1\), corresponding to \(\eta \in \{-\sqrt{ rac{t}{s}}, -\sqrt{ rac{s}{t}}\}\). Now look for all eigenvalues \( heta\) corresponding to \(\eta \in \mathbb{C} \setminus \{0, 1, -1, \sqrt{st}, rac{1}{\sqrt{st}}, -\sqrt{ rac{t}{s}}, -\sqrt{ rac{s}{t}}\}\). For \(1 \le i \le d - 1\), substituting \(a_i = s - 1\), \(b_i = st\), \(c_i = 1\), and \( heta - (s - 1) = \sqrt{st}(\eta + \eta^{-1})\) turns the recurrence for \(u_i( heta)\) into a constant-coefficient linear recurrence

\[st\,u_{i+1}( heta) - \sqrt{st}(\eta + \eta^{-1})u_i( heta) + u_{i-1}( heta) = 0,\]

whose characteristic quadratic has roots \( rac{\eta}{\sqrt{st}}\) and \( rac{\eta^{-1}}{\sqrt{st}}\). Matching the initial values \(u_0( heta) = 1\) and \(u_1( heta) = rac{ heta}{s(t + 1)}\) gives the closed formula

\[u_l( heta) = rac{t(\eta^{l+1} - \eta^{-l-1}) + (s - 1)\sqrt{s^{-1}t}(\eta^l - \eta^{-l}) - (\eta^{l-1} - \eta^{-l+1})}{(t + 1)(\eta - \eta^{-1})(\sqrt{st})^l}\]

for every \(l \in \{0, 1, \dots, d\}\).

Third, impose the minimal-polynomial boundary equation at layer \(d\) (using \(a_d = k - c_d\)):

\[-c_d u_{d-1}( heta) + ( heta - k + c_d)u_d( heta) = 0.\]

Substituting the formula for \(u_{d-1}( heta)\) and \(u_d( heta)\) and dividing by \( heta - s(t + 1) eq 0\) simplifies this boundary equation to

\[t(\eta^{d+1} - \eta^{-d-1}) + (c_d + s - 1)\sqrt{s^{-1}t}(\eta^d - \eta^{-d}) + (c_d - 1)(\eta^{d-1} - \eta^{-d+1}) = 0.\]

This equation factors cleanly in both parities of \(n\). When \(n = 2d\) is even, we have \(c_d = t + 1\), and the equation factors as

\[(\eta^d - \eta^{-d}) igl(s + t + (\eta + \eta^{-1})\sqrt{st} igr) = 0.\]

Because \(\eta otin \{-\sqrt{ rac{t}{s}}, -\sqrt{ rac{s}{t}}\}\), the second factor is nonzero, forcing \(\eta^d = \eta^{-d}\), or \(\eta^{2d} = \eta^n = 1\) with \(\eta eq \pm 1\). Since \(\eta = e^{2\pi i l / n}\) and \(\eta^{-1} = e^{-2\pi i l / n}\) give the same eigenvalue \( heta\), these \(n - 2\) roots of unity produce the remaining \(d - 1\) distinct eigenvalues of \(\Gamma\):

\[ heta_l = s - 1 + 2\sqrt{st}\cos\left( rac{2\pi l}{n} ight) \qquad (l \in \{1, 2, \dots, d - 1\}).\]

When \(n = 2d + 1\) is odd, we have \(c_d = 1\) and \(s = t\), and dividing by \(t\) factors the boundary equation as

\[(\eta + 1)(\eta^d - \eta^{-d-1}) = 0.\]

Because \(\eta eq -1\), this forces \(\eta^{2d+1} = \eta^n = 1\) with \(\eta eq 1\). Pairing \(\eta = e^{2\pi i l / n}\) with \(\eta^{-1}\) produces the remaining \(d\) distinct eigenvalues of \(\Gamma\):

\[ heta_l = s - 1 + 2s\cos\left( rac{2\pi l}{n} ight) \qquad (l \in \{1, 2, \dots, d\}).\]

Fourth, apply Biggs' multiplicity condition: because the multiplicity \(f( heta_l) = v / \sum_{i=0}^d k_i u_i( heta_l)^2\) is a positive integer, the denominator \(S(l) = \sum_{i=0}^d k_i u_i( heta_l)^2\) must be a rational number for every \(l\).

When \(n = 2d + 1\) is odd (so \(s = t > 1\)), summing \(\sum_{i=0}^d k_i u_i( heta_l)^2\) gives

\[S_{ ext{odd}}(l) = rac{n}{t + 1}\left(1 + rac{(t - 1)^2}{2t igl(1 - \cos rac{2\pi l}{n} igr)} ight) \in \mathbb{Q}.\]

Because \(t > 1\), the numerator \((t - 1)^2\) is nonzero, so rationality of \(S_{ ext{odd}}(1)\) at \(l = 1\) forces \(\cos igl( rac{2\pi}{n} igr) \in \mathbb{Q}\). By the rational cosine lemma (\(n \in \{2, 3, 4, 6\}\)), no odd value of \(n \ge 5\) is possible.

When \(n = 2d\) is even, summing \(\sum_{i=0}^d k_i u_i( heta_l)^2\) for \(l \in \{1, 2, \dots, d - 1\}\) gives

\[S(l) = rac{n}{t + 1}\left(1 + rac{s(t - 1)^2 + t(s - 1)^2 + 2(s - 1)(t - 1)\sqrt{st}\cos rac{2\pi l}{n}}{4st \sin^2 rac{2\pi l}{n}} ight) \in \mathbb{Q}.\]

To eliminate \(\sqrt{st}\cos rac{2\pi l}{n}\) even before knowing whether \(\sqrt{st}\) is rational, add \(S(1)\) and \(S(d - 1)\). Because \( rac{2\pi(d - 1)}{n} = \pi - rac{2\pi}{n}\), we have \(\sin^2 rac{2\pi(d - 1)}{n} = \sin^2 rac{2\pi}{n}\) and \(\cos rac{2\pi(d - 1)}{n} = -\cos rac{2\pi}{n}\) (and at \(d = 2\), where \(d - 1 = 1\), \(\cos rac{2\pi}{4} = 0\) anyway), so the cosine terms cancel:

\[S(1) + S(d - 1) = rac{2n}{t + 1}\left(1 + rac{s(t - 1)^2 + t(s - 1)^2}{4st \sin^2 rac{2\pi}{n}} ight) \in \mathbb{Q}.\]

Since at least one of \(s, t\) is greater than \(1\), we have \(s(t - 1)^2 + t(s - 1)^2 > 0\), so rationality of \(S(1) + S(d - 1)\) forces \(\sin^2 rac{2\pi}{n} \in \mathbb{Q}\), and hence

\[\cos\left( rac{4\pi}{n} ight) = 1 - 2\sin^2\left( rac{2\pi}{n} ight) = \cos\left( rac{2\pi}{d} ight) \in \mathbb{Q}.\]

Applying the rational cosine lemma to \(d\) forces \(d \in \{2, 3, 4, 6\}\), so \(n = 2d \in \{4, 6, 8, 12\}\).

Finally, suppose both \(s > 1\) and \(t > 1\), so \((s - 1)(t - 1) eq 0\). Because \(d \in \{2, 3, 4, 6\}\), we already have \(\sin^2 rac{2\pi l}{n} = rac{1}{2} igl(1 - \cos rac{2\pi l}{d} igr) \in \mathbb{Q}\) for every \(l \in \{1, \dots, d - 1\}\), so rationality of \(S(l)\) requires \(\sqrt{st}\cos rac{2\pi l}{n} \in \mathbb{Q}\) for all \(l \in \{1, \dots, d - 1\}\):

Hexagons (\(n = 6\), \(d = 3\)). Taking \(l = 1\) gives \(\cos rac{2\pi}{6} = rac{1}{2}\), so \(\sqrt{st} \in \mathbb{Q}\) and \(st\) is a perfect square.

Octagons (\(n = 8\), \(d = 4\)). Taking \(l = 1\) gives \(\cos rac{2\pi}{8} = rac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\), so \(\sqrt{2st} \in \mathbb{Q}\) and \(2st\) is a perfect square.

Dodecagons (\(n = 12\), \(d = 6\)). Taking \(l = 2\) gives \(\cos rac{4\pi}{12} = rac{1}{2}\) and hence \(\sqrt{st} \in \mathbb{Q}\), whereas taking \(l = 1\) gives \(\cos rac{2\pi}{12} = rac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) and hence \( rac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\sqrt{st} \in \mathbb{Q}\), impossible since \(\sqrt{3}\) is irrational. Thus any finite generalized dodecagon of order \((s, t)\) must have \(s = 1\) or \(t = 1\).

docs.title: Eigenvalue catalogue and worked test on a hexagon and a pentagon
docs.text:
Collecting \(\theta_0 = s(t + 1)\), the roots-of-unity eigenvalues \(\theta_l = s - 1 + 2\sqrt{st}\cos\frac{2\pi l}{n}\) (\(1 \le l \le d - 1\)), and \(\theta_d = -t - 1\) gives all \(d + 1\) distinct eigenvalues of \(\Gamma\) for each of the three even polygon families:
